VALENTINES. Once more the shops are full of valentines! And some are sweet ones, Fall of food wishes out of which love shines; And some are passiOn-tinged with deep designs; Some merely neat ones; Others, with nought to read between the lines— No inner meanings and no secret signs— Are most discreet ones! Oh! in this world, where grief with joy so twines, This great, full world, with secret springs and mines ' Fixed loves and fleet ones, What must there hang on all these valentines. Sweet, neat discreet ones? Casselrs lanuty itaaazine.
WILFRID Woomem.

Avoid passion and excitement; &moment's anger may be fatal. Learn to say no; not snappishly, but firmly and res- Peefully. Thirteen is not an unlucky number when you hold all the trump cards in a game of whist. Think nothing in conduct unimportant or indifferent. Try to see yourself through the eyes of those around

you. She, "I like this place immensely since they have the new Frerch chef." He (weak in his French,but generous to a fault), " Waitah, bring chef for two." A French country burying-ground has over its en- trance gate the following Hiberniap notice:—" Only the dead, who live in this parish, are buried here." • Mistress to servant, "Did you tell those ladies at the door that I was not at home?" Servant. " Yis, mum." Mistress.• "What did they say?" 'Servant, "How
fortinit ! " Tea eller, "Have animals a capacity for affection ? " Class, "Nearly all." Teacher, "Now, which animal possesses the greatest attachment for man ? " Class, •

Woman." "Don't let it happen again; that's all!" said Johnny's Mother, when she heard that he had played truant. "It didn't happen"-80"" this time"—sob. "I did it on Purpose. 800, hoo, boo !" O'Kellv : "Is it breaking yer long neck ver afther in the dark ?" Dolan: "Sure and oi foind the matches." O'Kelly : "Then strike a bight and luk for them like a sensible person." Nervous old lady, on fifth floor of hotel: "Do you know, what precautions the proprietor of the hotel has taken against fire?" Porter: "Yes, mum; he has the house insured for twice what it's worth." An Irishwoman, confined in the House of Correction, lately received a letter from her friends informing her that her children were all well. In reply, she stated that she "had not received so much consolation since her husband died." -sr "I would like a position on the editorial staff of your journal," said Mr. Sliinwit, uncovering his slender head as he bowed before the great min. " There is no staff position vacant just now." said the editor kindly; but I can eive you a special assignment." "Yes e " Yes, indeed', and you're just the man for it. I want somebody to pass himceltoff as an imbecile, and get into the Home for Feeble-Minded to write up the abuses of the institu- tion. You needn't waste time in training; go just as you are." DRUGGIST'S ORDERS.—The following odd oilers ate extracted from a druggist's scrap-book :—Send me some of your essence you put people to sleep with when you ,cut their fingers off. I want something to take tobacco out of my mouth. Send me a baby's top to tenursine &We. An ounce of the smellidg stuff that goes through your brain. Something for a sore baby's eye. Enough ipecac to throw up a girl four years old. Enough anise seed to take the twist out of a dose of senna. Plaster for a man kilt with stitches. Something for a caustic woman. Something to knock a cold out of an old woman. Something for a woman with a bad cough and cannot cough. Something, I forget the name, but it is for a cure for a swelled woman's foot. For a man with a dry spit on him. For a woman whose appetite is loose on her. PLAY CENSORSIIIP.—A friend of mine came to me lately with a long face. He is a well-known dramatic author, and the Lord Chamberlain had just refused to licenSe.one of his plays. "Don't be unhappy," I said; Shakspere ale() had to submit to the censorship." He wouldn't believe it until! took down Delius, and showed him how the Master of the Revels cut out the scene in Westminster Hall in "Richard II." The Government of the day couldn't allow the deposition of a king to be re- presented on the stage. in "Hamlet," also, an allusion to the drinking habits of the Danes had to be omitted, the then King of Denmark being such a notorious drunkard that the words might have been regarded as offensive. In the "Merchant of Venice." again, Portia was not allowed to laugh at her Scottish wooer, for , I,ames I. was a Scot, and it was not to be tolerated that anyone should laugh at anything connected with Os Majesty; so the censor struck out "the Scottish lord" ' from Shakespere's text and substituted "the other lord." When I had shown my friend thus far he grew less miserable. It is always a satisfaction to teel that the greatest also suffer. If Shakspere were living now, and sent up a new play to be licensed, I wonder how the Earl of Lathom and Mr. Pigott would deal with the .manu- script.— Cassell's Saturday Journal. HOUSE-BOATS IN SIAM. —At 'the present day the Siamese of Bankok may be said to be almost amphibious. Most of their life is passed on the water, and nearly all of their animal food they get from it. Except about the king's palace, horses are rarely seen, and carriages were formerly equally unknown. Canoes and boats age the ordinary modes of conveyance, and one or other is an absolute necessary to every household. A child is early trained to navigate it, so that men, women, and children use 'the oar, the paddle, and the rudder almost intuitively. Even the Chinese have left their sedan behind them, and, in common with the Siamese, take kindly to boat-life. The waters are covered with barges Of all sorts, from the skiff, to USD the language of a modern writer, "scarcely large enough to hold a doe, to the magnificently adorned barge which is honoured with the presence of royalty; from the shabbiest canoe hewn out of the small trunk of a tree from the.jungle up to the roofed and curtained, the carved and gilded barque of the nobles—every rank and condition has its boats plying in endless activity night and day on the surface of the Menem waters." Bankok is, in a word, "a float- ing city," the limits of which on land it is at first sight) impossible to determine.—Countries of the World. THE EXECUTION OF CRIMINALS BY ELECTRICITY.—The Medical Press and Circrlar in an article upon electricity as a means of effecting executions instead of hanging, says that Mr. Edison is reported to have declined on Drin- ciple to place his technical knowledge at the service of the reformers; but a contrivance known as'the'Hayes Garrison apparatus has been designed, which promises to attain the desired end. It consists of a copper band, which takes the place of the laurel crown on the brow of the condemned person, and presses strotigly on the nape of the neck. A zinc plate, on which the prospective vic- tim stands being the other electrode. On the contact being established death is instantaneous. The apparatus designed by M. Mendez resembles the above, except that it is in gutta-percha and the poles press on either temple. Two other systems are known as the Jablochkoff and the Paget. It is estimated that a battery of 500 cells would be strong enough for the purpose; and, as it could be used for more productive purposes when not requisi- tioned by the law, the cost per seance would be but small. The article concludes—" The present condition of elec- trical science, however, does not inspire confidence. We can put up with an occasional • wobble' in the electric 1 light, or an occasional delay or error in the dispatch of a telegram, but there must be no 'wobbling' when life has to be disposed of." FLAREOT.ET V. PIANO.—Let me give another instance of "fellowship" unconcern for undergraduittes—not so deadly, but not insignificant. A senior Oxford Don "kept" in the rooms above mine. He was very musical, and had a resonant grand piano on which his learned leisure led him generally to beg,in:playing at aboutten every morning. By that hour I was supposed to bet sny books. Every note of this performing "fellow's" instrument sounded in my room. Reading was impos- sible. The man drove .ne half mad. Of course I ought to have civilly remonstrated (the authorities extinguished a youth who began to learn the cornet, with his window open, at about the same hour), but some information reached me that in my case remonstrance would be sse&te of energy.. My man was not an undergraduate, and in Os musical utterances did not, like the cornet player, address the whole college. He was, I suppose, reported to be unapproachable. So I tried another line of action, and one evening brought a flageolet. Next morning I laid it down by my inkstand and began to read "conic sections.". He began a "fugue." I put down my pen and piped Marbrough s'en va-t-en guerre." I should observe that to this marked and pene- trating melody the youth of the place used to sing "We won't go home till morning." Presently my Don stag- gered and stopped. I stopped. In about ten minutes he began again. So did I. This intermittent instru- mental duet went on every forenoon for nearly a week, and was (on my side) watched with much interept by many friends. At last indications of defeat were per- ceptible. On the fourth or fifth day, when my man found that he could not touch his piano without starting my pipe, I heard him slam down his instrument, stamp *out the floor, and presently bang the door, having gone out. I was much encouraged, and used not only to play bits of tunes in moments of leisure, but left a , standing note on my table by the flageolet requesting any friend who might come in to do his best. At last our enraged musician appealed to the authorities against me. I could only reply that while I admired his efficiency and regretted my own want of skill, I hoped to do better in time and with more practice. The business ended in my victory: be promised not to play in the morning' I did the same. And he was not such a bad fellow after all, for when he was beaten' we shook hands, and he asked me to "wine." I believe that there are approaches to a better understanding between the elders and young men at college than existed in my time.—Good Words. The FATHER of Mr. Daniel Lineham, Mallow, County Cork, Ireland, suffered from rheumatism and was unable to find relief for six years. From one application of St. Jacobs Oil he received marked benefit, and in a week all pain left him and he was cured. • •

div.head: PA#ERS FOR THE PEOPLE.
div.p: PA#ERS FOR THE PEOPLE.

• BY HUGH BETTE. IV.—INDIAN CLUBS; When a peaceable citizen spe[iks of a,'" club" we naturally infer that he means a civilised organisation of human beings, and I hereby lodge my protest against those men of an athletic persuasion Using the word loosely without an adjective, such as barbarian Abyssinian, or Indian. If you are in a fog about this read on.

I believe it is the duty nf every man who seeks medical advice to follow the advice up after he gets it. The medical advice given to me for indigestion was "mild exercise," but as this, with different individuals, embraces everything between shovelling coals ino and walking. round the back garden, I demanded more definite details. I was then advised to learn,the dumb bell and Indian club exercises; the dumb bells first. and, as my muscles began to show through my clothing, the Indian clubs were to follow. I shook a pair of dumb bells at .a portrait of the Grand Old Man in my bedroom till it looked quite mournful, but the exercise didn't digest my indigestion; and, to tell you the truth, it got very tame, so I turned my attention to tkose articles called briefly, by the men protested against, "clubs," but named by Christian communities "Indian clubs ;" possibly to 'distinguish them as a heathen prochfction. The Indian club is a piece of wood turned something like the shape of a champagne bottle, and varying in size according to the suicidal propensities of the club- bist ; but my opinion is that any piece of wood with a handle shaped to it, and long and/heavy enough to knock the legs from under a man, will do just as well. I bought a pair nicely polished, however, weighing about 41bs. each. I felt certain that the club exercise wouldn't be near so tame as bells, which proved to be correct. I pause here to remark emphatically that it is not tame. • My friend Crofter can, almost cut the alphabet out with a pairof Indian clubs. I talked the matter over with him, and he fixed an evening for me to bring my clubs to his house, and be,shown a few evolutions. He took a club in each hand, and the different circles they made round him quite enchanted me, and all without so much as him getting red in the face. He next did what he called a "simple movement" for me to copy, which consisted of making two clubs rotate so ,that they looked like nine or ten. • - He then handed them to me, and put me in position. I wanted to start with one at a time, but he said this had the very detrimental effect of developing one side of the body more than the other, which' is very reasonable when you come to look at it. As I took off my coat Crofter's mother-in-law got up to go out, remarking that she couldn't bear to see any- body hurt. I thought I could stick to those clubs without letting them fly out of my hands andjiitting the spectatork and said so; but she went out all the same. "Now," said Crofter, "don't try to push the clubs round; after you have started them, let each one swing round from the first momentum." I understood him perfectly, as I am well up in momentum. I held both clubs up in front of me, in a vertical position according to directions, and Crofter shotted, "One, two, three." The momentum of the first club exhausted itself on my right big toe, and the second club was brought up short against Ole first. I should undoubtedly have howled if I had beemby myself, but I mustered up a ghastly smile, and prepared for a second effort, stimu- lated by cries of "Well done," "Very good," Sze., from Crofter, and wondering inwardly how much of the toe was left, I got the clubs up again, and executed a sort of triangle in front of me, which Crofter pronounced to be excellent. He next showed me how to swing them round behind my back, and for a third time I got in position. "Now," said Crofter, "mind what I said about checking the circle half-way." They started. I grieve to state that I couldn't help checking them. Crofter explained that the reason they stopped against the calves of my legs was that I leaned too much forward. I raised an idiotic smile, and said I would go home and practice what he had shown me; but he said I had nothing to practice off yet, and then he proceeded to convince me that he never saw a fellow get on so well before. I was thinking of the rubbing bottle at home, and that the sooner it was applied the less would be the danger of mortification. Crofter said the next movement was swinging one club round before and the other behind at the same time. I suddenly remembered an engagement, and promised to be back in half-an-hour. He said he was sure I wasn't one of those soft fellows who didn't give a thing a fair trial. Pwas beginning to think that the longer I continued this practice the softer I should go, physically at any rate, but I couldn't resist tha temptation to try that double motion. I think I could have get the front club round very nicely if I had had time to look after the back one, but I was too excited to notice the path of each of those clubs. The way they travelled all over my body was truly wonderful, butt,l held on like grim death, till I felt as if I was standing on my hands, and the clubs were being whirled around by' my feet. The shouts of encouragement from Crofter seemed to come up from a far distant cellar, and when at last one club stopped suddenly on the top of my head, I thought the kitchen boiler had burst. Crofter spoke to me, but I was absorbed in astronomy, then I distinguished that he was saying something about not having tried the "triple backward and for- ward motion reversed." I sat Mown in a chair to think. "Do you feel fagged ?" asked Crofter. I don't know whether he used the word fagged in the sense I took it or not, but I was fagged. The only may I could tear myself away from him was by leaving my clubs and promising to call in again shortly for another lesson. I shouldn't like to suspect that he has my life insured. I not only haven't called since, but I have made engage- ments for every evening during the next two years. When I do take any more lessons on Indian clubs, I shall either have a feather bed strapped round me, or put my arms through the skylight ind do the evolutions outside. You will naturally feel interested about the indiges- tion. I cannot say whether it is better or worse till the plasters come off, and the swelling in my shoulder blades have gone down. Anyway, if the symptoms reappear, I shall return to the tame dumb bells, or climb over some wall covered with broken glass, or take some mild exer- cise of that sort; not Indian clubs.

div.head: T ITE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 18, 1888:
div.p: T ITE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 18, 1888:
ST. BARNADAS CHURCH TEA TARTY.

The annual congregational tea party in connec- tion with this church was lfeld on Tuesday evening in the Public Hall, when over 300 persons sat down to tea. At a subsequent meeting the chair was occupied by the Rev. G. Anton, the vicar, and amongst those also present were the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Sutton), Councillor John Pierpoint, Mrs. and Miss Allton, Mrs: T. Mor- ris, Mr. S. H. Holmes (vicar's warden), Mr. E. J. Denham (peoples warden), Mr. Brown (head schoolmaster), Mrs. Bfown, and Miss• Parsons (schoolmistress). In the course of am address Mr. Allton thanked those ladies and gentlemen., who had assisted in the task of keeping the work of the parish afloat during the year, and the churchwar- dens, sidemen, and Sunday sehool teachers who had given such valuable assistance. The gentry of the town and neighbourhood had been most helpful to him ; in fact, without their asestance they could not g'et on and it was a pleasure to him to be able to announce that sone tp whom he had appealed for help had refused it. Ho still regarded his parish, after four years of labour in it, as a missionary parish, for missionaries were required to go frpns house to house to help forward the work, that one, unaided, could not do, When he first came to thetown, four years ago, there was no endow- • 'ment for the church, and there was not even a penny in the poor box. They got the church endowed, and ob- tained land from the Hon. Leopold Powys, who had been a good friend. They collected money with which to build a school, and had the church comfortably seated throughout, principally through the kindness of Mrs. T. Mogi& Lettelos had appeared in the newspapers to the et that the church was being monopolised, and that it was not free ; but he wished to say that the church was free. When people came to church regularly, they should, he thought, occupy the same seets,'but beyond these every placp in the church was free. Among the friends who had given him able assistance in his ;work he mentioned the Mayor and Mayoress, Mr. and Mrs T. Morris, and Mr. and Mrs Pierpoint. They now owed £321, and they were intending to get up ibazaar or sale of work to raise the amount required. The parish. con- tained some six thousand people, and he should like some to come forward and offer their services as lay helpers. The Hen. Leopold Powys had let him have land for a vicarage near the church, and notwithstanding their difficulties, they had succeeded in raising £1,050 towards the beilding of a new vicarage. It would thus be seep that although they were few in number and poor, they were not without life.—Councillor J. PIER- POINT proposed a vote of thanks to the ladies who had presided at the tea tables, and to all who had assisted in various ways in connection with the gathering. He had no doubt, he said, that the debt new existing on the schools would soon be cleared off. The infant schools had been paid for, and for that they must thank Sir Gilbert Greenall.—The proposition was seconded by the MAYOR, who, having expressed the hope that the debt referred to would soon be defrayed, said, that he considered that these tea parties served a useful purpose, because they had a tendency to bring the parishioners together.--The resolution was then agreed to.—During the evening songs were given by Mr. Charles McD,owell, Miss Holly, and Mr. J. Mercer. Mr. George Riley acted as accompanist. Dancing was subsequently indulged in.—The following is a list of those who gave trays : Sir Gilbert Greene'', Bart., M.P. Lady Greenall, Sir A. B. IValker, Mrs Stanton, the hey. W. Quekett, Mrs Quekett, Mrs Lyon, Mrs Charlton Parr, the Rev. Ca no Whitley, Mrs W. C. Jones, Mrs Stubs, Mr. J. Cros- field, the Mayor and Mayoress of Warrington, Mrs Sher- ratt, Mrs J. Pierpoint, Mrs Morris, Miss Tiddy, Mr. R. Davies, Mr—P. Leigh, Mr. J. Tinsley, Alderman Harri- son, Mrs Rowson, Messrs. Milling and Co., Mrs Adams, theTanning'Company, the Grand Clothing Hall Com- pany, Messrs. Carter and Sons, Mr. W. Gibson, Mr. John White, Mrs Robinson, Mrs Evans, MrsPlatt, Mrs Holmes, Mrs Denham, Mrs Roscoe, Mrs J. Woods, Mrs Proud, Mrs Stringer, the Whitecross Wire and Iron Company, Limited.

Th. shrewd manager was of •course delighted to make his acquaintance, gave him full particulars of his plans, telling him among other things that he had engaged the National Theatre in the city oft Mexico for a month, from December 15th. The next thing Mr: Abbey heard of hfs entertaining companion Was that he had gone to the city of Mexico, had repre- sented himself to Mr. Mayer, Mr. Abbey's agent, had sold places in advance to hear Patti, had pocketed many thousand dollars, and had disappeared. As usual in the genial month of March the Queen will hold drawing rooms at I3uckingham Palace. It is a pitiful sight, when the east wind is blowing, to see the long line of carriages, with foolish , women shivering in broad daylight in evening dress. There is, however, some hope that , possibly valuable lives may be saved this year. ,Invitations i have been issued as usual, but it s understood that if anything happens to ,the Crown. P.rince the Drawing Room will be postponed, even at ten minuternotice— It is direful to tdiin,k of a lady having involved husband or father in the cost of a drawing rodm dress, and having been occupied since early dawn in arraying herself, should, just as she was stepping into the carriage to go to Bucking- him Palace, receive a telegram withdrawing the in- vitations. But there are even worse things • than that, a fatal cold for instance.

div.head: OUR LONDON ;LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON ;LETTER.
LONDON. THIIISDAY NIGHT.

The condition of affairs in the House of Commons was varied to-night by a congregation of attractive+ speakers. The benches rapidly filled up. the air be- came electric, and it was much easier to believe that we were still in the earliest days of an impor- tant session. For the rest, the state of things has been unprecedented. Even in oviinary times the House of Commons is pretty sure to be filled up dur- ing the first fortnight of the session. But these are niit ordinary tittles. With a regular procession of members of Padiament marching from prisons, with members arrested on the very steps of the House, it was reasonable to look for an exceptional state of excitement. But the reverse has been the case. At no time since the Address was ntoved, with the exception of this evening's sitting, has the House presented anything like a crowded appear- ance. For the most part it has been half empty, and more than once the debate on the Address has been threatened with collapse. This is due in a large measure to the attitude as- sumed by the leaders of the two wings of the Op- position. Mr. Gladstone took an early opportunity of deprecating anything like obstruction, express- ing his hearty desire to co-operate in bringing abodt what he called "a legislative session." Mr. Parnell, in the remarkably able speech he delivered on Monday, took the same line. He even went fur- ther, promising actively to assist the Government in carrying their legislation, as progress in that direction meant the nearer, accomplishment of Home Rule. The result is seen in the present con- dition of the House. Instead of a succession of ex- citing scenes, we have a series of speeches, which are bat echoes of things that have been said over and over again in ,the recess. According to present appearances, the Address will be voted to-morrow night, the period of discussion falling far short of that occupied in recent years. The House has, i moreover, habitually risen n good time. Not once since it met has the Speaker been in the chair whea one o'clock struck. A.n unwonted atmosphere of apathetic peace prevails, which, unless ruffled by some maladroit aim on the part of the Government, may last throughout the seapon. The prevalent state of things encourages ord Hartington in an attitude very agreeable to him. As there is nothing going forward in the House, theie is no occasion for his attendance, and he makes the most of his opportunities. Sometimes he may be seen peering in at the Hpuse through the glass door under the clock. But, having thus mastered the situation, he walks away again, and is seen no more through the sitting. It can be well understood that the house of Commons is ao de-

lightful resort for him in th_e present circumstances. When he is there, he sits stolidly aloof from the vast majority of the partyawhose confidence he mice possessed in the fullest degree. When he made his appearance on the first day of the session, it was from ttie Conservative side that welcoming cheers arose, his 'old friends sitting in saddened silence. If Lord Hartington, like Mr. Goschen, had made up his mind to cross the Rubicon and take his seat in the Conservative camp, this demonstration Would be well enough. But to a man of sensitive nature,' it cannot be altogether a very comfortable thing to sit on one side of the House "and be cheered from the other. It is, moreover, depressing to sit in literal isolation on a crowded bench. Mr. Chamber- lain, when at home, is a pretty frequent attendant at the House of Commons, and Lord Hartington was wont to find someone with whom he could chat, and so avoid some of the awkwardness of the situation. But now if he goes there he is pretty sure to find himself alone, even the faithful Mr. Heneage showing this session a disposition to shirk the duty of putting in an appearance. Sir H. James was in his place lyt Monday. But his ex- perience was not such as to induce a •regular attendance. In his °baste to help the Government in the privilege debate, he blundered with quite unusual stupidity, and amid the delighted °beers of his offi frjAnds drew upon himself one of the most scathing clistigations that Mr. Gladstone has ever administered to a member of the House. Sir Henry James has not visited the House since he safely got out of it on Monday. • The growing spirit of stern resentment against former members of the Liberal party who are now, helping a Conservative Government to coerce Ire- land is strikingly shown in Mr. Jesse. Collings's ex- pulsion from the chair of the Allotments and Small Holdings Association, effected yesterday. Mr. Col- lings was the founder of this association in far off days when he was, according to his lights, working with.tho Liberal party for the amelioration of the lot of the masses. Four years the association has now existed, and every year Mr. Collings has, as a matter of course, been re-elected president. Yester- day he was deposed, only three hands in a meeting of representative men, being held up in his favour. The proceedings were marked throughout by the extremeet courtesy. 'All the good things it waspos- sibleo say of Mr. Collings were uttered with em- phasis. Only the Liberals present engaged upon an essentially .Liberal work, would not consent any longer to go forward under the nominal leadership of a gentleman* whose endeavours are pledged to keeping a Conservative Government in office and , Mr. Gladstone out oft. Some time ago the Cham- berlain family, more imperious or mote far-seeing than Mr. Jesse Collings, withdrew from the isso- elation, taking with them their aggregate sulsscrip- tion of .£ll9 ss; whereupon two or three other members planked down a sum of .£5O, so that the association was, financially, much richer for the secession. In order to make it just twice as rich, Mr. Brunner has now promised an additional £lO subscription. This action on the part of the asso- ciation, coming as it does close upon the reception Mr. Jesse Collings met with from his constituents Birmingham the other day, is assurejly the poli- tical death knell of the .Dissentient Liberals. If they want to remain in political life, they must go over, bag and ba.cgage, to the Conseriative side, and take their chance in Parliamentary contests against regular members of that party. Walking along the Strand to-day, I witnessed a very remarkable scene. The thoroughfare was, as usual, crowded to its utmost capacity. A throng hurrying east met one pushing west, and the road- way was almost a block of 'busses, cabs, and carts. As I walked along towards Charing Cross, I became conscious of a curious movement in the crowd Everyone was looking in a particular direction to- wards the middle of the road. The current, neither east nor west, stopped, people being too busy to waste time in unnecessary halt. But the procession slowed, and necks were craned and'facea turned all upon one foetus. Following the direction, I dis- covered Mr. Gladstone nimbly threading his way through the dangerously moving mass of vehicles. A youth of seventeen could not have tripped more lightly across the roadway, dodging the horses, going one way, and changing his course when he got into the other current. He was dressed in a quaintly-cut garment, half cloak, half overcoat, which, if not made at home, must have been the earnest effort of a village tailor. He walked with brisk step, his head held straight up, looking with interest at the contents of the shop windows, and apparently unconscious that he was the centre of observation in the busiest thoroughfare in the world. An old friend of the London police is now in trouble in New York. This is Benson, the famous forger and swindler, Whose chronicles are swritten large in English criminal records. Only last autumn Benson was released from a long term of penal servi- tude in connection with what were known as the "turf frauds." He thereupon took • a trip to the United States', and was very early at work again. On the way he found on the Umbria a fellow passenger in Mr. Abbey, the American theatre managam. Mr. Abbey had engaged Patti for a tour in the United States and Mexico. Benson, who passed underthe name of Bourton, introduced himself to Mr. Abbey

'• The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 89 cases, 70 of which we old and 19 new.— Mr. BLACKRUSST, in moving the adoption of the report, said he was glad to say that the number of eases was op, the decrease in comparison with last year. He thought they had about ten cases fewer the day before than at the same time last year, and 20 less than the year before. Jottaut seconded the proposition, which was agreed to.

,7aCCINATION. The Cuins said he had received returns from all the vaccination Meows of the Union.—Mr. W..Houosrrow asked what position the Union was in with regard to arrears in vaccination.—The CLERK said there were always a few arrears.—Mr. W. HorrorrroN thought it was imperative on them to see that vaccination was looked after. The reports they got from Sheffield where ravages from smallpox had taken place owing to neglect in vaccination or re-vaccination made it ne.deesary for them, as the authority for. enforcing vaccination, to see that it was done for their own and the public protection. —Mr. CIARICI begged to say that vaccination was no protection against smallpox. He had studied the figures with regard to Sheffield very closely sad, like many other figures before them, they were not to be relied upon. He should not like to waste the time of the Board that morning in prbvinglhat figures in the past had not been satisfactory—he would not like tip go into details, but he would say that vaccination was no proteCtion from smallpox, and therefore as one member of that Board he thought the statement Mr. Sutton had made was quite satisfactory as regarded vaccination, for it was perfectly useless as regarded protection.—Mr. Jot- au said he should certainly support Mr. Houghton, and he hoped. the clerk would instruct the officers to see that vaccination was-kept up, for he thought it " was a great protectioa.—The Cum' should be inclined to say that the officers were very fairly doing their duty, but of course in some districts difficulties were experienced. Mr. Houghton would see the details in the officers' re- ports, and W there was anything in them tie wished to call attention to he could do so.—Later on in the meet- ing Mr. W. HOUGHTON said he saw from the reports that in Mr. Cooper's district (Newton) there were something like 18 per cent of children unvaccinated, while in some outlying districts there was only something like one per cent.—Mr. RATCLIFFB said if Mr. Houghton re- ferred to Newton he dare say he could satisfactorily ex- plain to him the reason. (Laughter.)—Mr. W. Hones- TON did net know whether Mr. Rateliffe's reasons would be sufficient, and he would suggest that the clerk write to Mr. Cooper for an explanation.—This suggestion was agreed to and the matter dropped.

Thu com- mittee also authorised similar alterations of the veitila- tion, &c., at the lodge. The committee approved of the alteration of ' the school partitions by Mr. Kellet, of Earlast•wn, joiner, for the sum of £l2 1.25, the work to be done to the approval of Mr. W. Owen, and an order was directed accordingly. The committee was informed by Mr. Mines of his intention to apply on his own behalf, and that of Mrs. Mines, the matron, with a view to their pecuniary advantage, fof offices in another poor law Union corresponding to those they held at Padgate school 4. The committee, whilst regretting the prospect of losing their services, had pleasure in recommending that a very high testimonial be given, and it was also recommended that the clerk be instructed to prepare such a testimonial and sign it on behalf of tho Board and the committee.—The CLERK said the chairman of the Board (the Rev. G. F. Roberts) called upon him on Monday, and said that in consequence of the death of his mother at Carnarvon he would be unable to attend that meeting, but had he deem so he would have been glad to support the testimonial to Mr. Mines.—On the motion of Mr. GRSEXING seconded by Mr. ISHERWOOD, the minutes were adopted.

div.head: CHAPTER I.
div.p: CHAPTER I.
THE BANDITS.
Mr. Stanhope had been very careful when lila boys were still young to put their names down for one or two of the best London clubs. He was a man who fully . . .
believed in association and companionship having ail imnieni3e deal to do with forming a young man's
character.

It was, therefore, quite without his advice, in fact without his knowledge, that Ferdinand enrolled his same as one of the Balydits a proprietary club having its whereabouts in a quiet turning out of Pall Mall.

Steady going, essentially correct Henry Stanhope would probably never have known that there was such a club had he not been blessed or cursed with a son who was resolved not to saunter monotonously along the straight paths of life. Yet among the Bandits Ferdinand was generally to be found when he man- . .

aged to get leave—from Hounslow and slip up to town; very frequently on these occasioas not even putting man appearance in Eaton-square. The Bandits, be it understbod, were by no means Bohemian ; though a few of the Cite from that country had strayed among them, they were for the most part offshoot's of the upper ten. He lounges in there one night in May looking so morose and taciturn that his greatest intimates scarcely know him, for Verdinand, as a rule, is a jocose and merry fellow and does not allow the cares of life to sit very heavily upon him. Neither is he by any means of a seoretive turn of mild, and usually tells his troubles, when the chronic state of money difficulties in which he is involved becomes a trouble, pretty freely to those whom he considers his friends.

To-night, however, he is most reserved ; neither taunts nor chaff will draw from him one word as to what has gone amiss with him. "Leave him, leave him," says the Hon. Julius "he has only caught the disease at last. Can't you see he is Li love? What's the use of bully- ing a fellow 1"

"Wrong for once iu ywn• life. Blain," answered Ferdinand, "I never felt mu.. “rilike being in love than Ido at this moment. I'm out of temper, that's all. Surely I have as much right to be out of temper, if I chose, as any other infernal idiot. . . .

, "0, well, if you don't mind calling yourself an infernal idiot, we'll forgive you," cried Mr. Blain, laughing; "but you ought to know by this time, Ferdinand, that jollity is one of the pass words .ere, and that you should leave your ill temper in barracks, or at the Rag, or any other place where they like a little spleen. Come and forget how dis- agreeable she has been, my dear boy, and have s, gamble." "What the devil do you know about ' she ? What do you know about it, I should like to know. Go and gamble yourself. I won't touch a beastly card to- night." " Hullo, • hullo, has she been trying to make you give it up? We are beginning to discover at last where the shoe pinches. Don't marry a woman who starts by bullying you before marriage. My dear fellow, it is a mistake." Ferdinand looked at him in utter astonishment for a few seconds, and then burst out laughing. The persistency with which they imposed a love affair on him amused him, and as he had no intention whatever of telling them what had in reality upset his equili- brium, perhaps this excuse would do as well as any other. Own to the Bandits that his mother had been lecturing him and had perhaps, if only for a time,made him regret that weakness of his which she said was dragging his family down into mire—the very thought of such a thing was ont of the question. Take the Bandits as a body, notwithstanding the jollity and camaraderie which they professed, they could be scarcely designated as a set of good fellows ; and it was an evil hour in which Ferdinand Stanhope bad consented to become a member of the club, since the companionship of the men he met there was calcu- lated to considerably strengthen the vices already in- herent in his nature, while the society of noble, honourable men might have considerably improved his character, for Ferdinand, notwithstanding his big imposing appearance and grand blustering manners, was the weakest of the Stanhopes, and a few persuasive words would always lead him where neither Geoffery nor Irene would ever have been induced to follow.
Alas, that persuasion usually carries its greatest weight when it points to some down-hill pathway. . . . .

fo-day, however, it had been exerc'.sing itself for good, when it had fallen in kindly, loving pleadings from the lips of the only human being for whom Ferdinand professed as deep an affection as his natur- ally unloving nature was capable of. His one redeeming point was that .he loved his mother, but he would, indeed, have been almost inhuman if he bad been impervious to the con- sistent tenderness and gentleness with which Lady Fedora ever treated her children and their faults. Geoffrey's candid, straightforward character irri- tated Ferdinand; Irene's simple-hearted goodness he set down as childish; his sister counted for very little in. his life. . . . .

Mr. Stanhope had been quite right when he had at last carried the burden of Ferdinand's short-coming and laid them at Lady Fedora's feet, for she alone had any influence over the young soldier. The only fear was, had Mr. Stanhope done se soon enough? Was uot Ferdinand already so deeply plunged that it would- take far more than a mother's. rood advice to enable him to scramble back to the 4ltittide from which he had fallen! Had Lady Fedora for ftßloment dreamed of condescending to consult Mrs. Purvis on the subject of her son Ferdinand's affairs, the housekeeper might, had she chosen to unloose her tone, have not a little appalled the worthy parents of this most Unworthy scion. But the women, gentle and lowly, who, in their several ways, were devoted to Ferdinand, kept their own counsel. It is only in moments of great pressure that a high-bred woman like Lady Fedora makes a confidante of one in her service, and had she elected to do so now, it would probably have been Yrs. Knight she would have chosen to speak with. There was a kindliness and: simplicity in the nature of Phyllis's mother, which was much more in unison with Lady Fedora's feelings than the coarser and more common place attributes which Mrs. Purvis possessed. But with Ferdinand's affairs what had either of these women to do? Lady Fedora would have asked. Strange how little even the most carefully obser- vant mistresses know of the workings of life within their own establishments. Without a word, then, to anyone, strong in the belief of what his mother's love would effeez, Lady Fedora went through a somewhat trying inter- view with Ferdinand. The impression left on her mind at its conclusion was that she had decidedly gained some ground since she had made her un- happy boy see the error of his ways, and surely. no Stanhope, no manly Stanhope, as was her Perth- hand, but would, when he saw the danger in which his actions were placing not only himself but those he loved, at once face it and withstand every temptation which would lure him within its dreaded radius. • From what Ferdinand himself had said, and the affectionate, almost tender manner in which he had treated her, Lady Fedora had every reason to think his conversion, if so it may be called, not only probable 'but certain, and it was with a far lighter heart she entered Mr. Stanhope's study as Ferdinand closed the hall door and walked across the square, than Lady Fedora had expected ever to feel again, so depressed had she been by Mr. Stanhope's relations. As Ferdinand gvalked across the square Mrs. Puxvis watched him fro la an upper window. "What had happened ? "she wondered ; he looked so dejeeted and east down that it must be something very grave. Money was, in general, the only thing that worried Ferdinand. Yet he had not been up to see her even for two seconds. It was strange. By which it might almost have been inferred that / Mrs. Purvis was Ferdinand's "man of business." It was barely six o'clock when Ferdinand left his father's house, and nearly half-past .ten when he entered the abode of the Bandits. During those four hours many and conflicting emotions had been rending and torturing him. For the first hour no voice but that of the gentle Lady Fedora had been paramount ; but gradually its dulcet strains had been overpowered by rougher, louder notes, and by the time he had turned into the Military Club to dine, he had began to hear only the talk of the men he met there, and to wonder why he shwa* not be as other men were, only, perhaps, not so Wad as he had been of late. Ah, Lady Fedora, with all her deep anxiety about Ferdinand, could scarcely gauge the depth of that bad- nese. He ate his dinner in a morose mood, without s)eaking to anso ae, but he heard talk going on around —turf, boating, cricket, balls. Ferdinand, shook him- self, and morbidness increasing as his mother's voice seemed to die further and further into the distance, he asked himself what he was that he should be asked to give up all these pleasant things to please a woman ; surely those men who chatted so easily of their plea- sures were not henpecked and worried as he vac.
".Come and play a I 00l at billiardsoStanhope," some, • one had asked him.

No, he. was hanged if be would, helated the sight of a billiard-table, and the click of the balls irritated him to frenzy—be glanced at the clock—a quarter to ten! He would go to the Bandits ; perhaps some congenial spirit there would cheer him; he had not promised he would not go there, only promised his mother he would not touch a card and would give up gambling. He owns what a fool he had been to promise such a thing, he was beginning to think so too. Had he not involved himself more heavily than anyone knew,and if he turned saint and retired into the cloisters of conversion, would he not be jeered at and held in contempt by his chums, who would consequently refuse him that temporary relief in the way of flying ' kites to which poor Ferdinand was already clinging with the usual tenacity of a sinking man? To laugh and look pleasant, then, when they were • torturing him on the subject of his evident annoyance, was evidently the best course to pursue, but to meet the views of his companions and actin accordance with his promise to his mother was by no means so easy since" come and have a gamble " was the refrain of their conversation, while " I will never touch a card again;" was the promise he uttered more than once under the strong pressure, as he was beginning to call it, which Lady Fedora had brought to bear upon him. Again and again they asked him to join them as usual, but the staunchness which was the strong cha- racteristic of most of the Stanhopes did not absolutely slumber even in this weak member, and he was re- solute—like most feeble people, brutally resolute— - that he would not touch a card that night, almost breaking down bis resolve to be politic with his com- - panions for help's sake, till Blain, who was, per- haps, as little vicious as any Bandit there, suggested that, it Ferdinand would net play at least he might come and watch them, and put a little money on for luck's sake. • _ _ _

_ To which change in the programme - Ferdinand at once agreed ; he had made no promise about looking on and betting. Good innocent Lady Fedora, she knew naught of this side of the picture—play- - ing at cards and having bad luck was her, idea of gambling.' Could she, about two hours later, have seen her Ferdinand, whom she fondly hoped was back at Hounslow, in bed and asleep, she would perchance have formed a new and by no means pleasing idea of how ruin may be effected by gambling without the touching of a single card. It was not of his mother that Ferdinand was • thinking then—he had long since forgotten her warnings; or, if occasionally a sad glance from . her soft eyes would seem for a moment to dwell on his downward course, ' it only seemed to madden him and make him play the higher, since nothing but excitement would silence the remorse that any thought of Lady Fedora would awaken in the future. Unhappy, misguided Ferdinand! From the moment he entered the haunt of the Bandits that night, hie ruin seemed inevitable, though, in accordance with the nsntl caprice of chance, for the first half hour after the play began he had backed the hand of a man called Dantri, a half foreigner, and an adept in games of skill, especially ecarte, and had won close upon eighty pounds; then the tide had turned, or, pirchance, Danti's brain was less clear, and by the - time the neighbouring clocks had struck one Ferdi- nand had lost two hundred and fifty pounds—" a mere nothing for a Stanhope," said one of the lookers on. They little knew to what a heavy total this sum had to be added, or at what a low ebb were already the fortunes of the Stanhopes. Ferdinand, however, knew it well, and though he - had been sipping alcohol all the evening, though no habitual drunkard, the announcement of the figure seemed at once to recall his wandering senses, and if he had looked jaded and out of spirits when he entered , the club, it was with such a dejected mien that he might have been on the very verge of suicide that he left it. The fresh night air to a degree, however, cooled his fevered brain, and ill- stead of returning to Eaton-square, where he had a latch key, to sleep, he wandered about the streets till morning, scarcely listing where he went or what occurred; in fact, he was more than once in danger of being taken up by the police for a suspicious cha- racter. _ . _

At last he reached the station, and sat down in the waiting-room till the first train to Hounslow should start. More than once he had thought of going to Eaton. square and having a talk with Mrs. Purvis, but he felt that he could not face his mother ; he mast com- municate with Purvis in some other way; besides' he did not wish his family to know that he had not re- turned to Hounslow on the preceding day, No. Bandit would tell them of that he felt sure; their league was a secret one. Light, however, cannot. usually be hid under a bushel, nor was Ferdinand's. A pair of observant eyes watched him at the station that morning, and though he did not see, and seeing would not have recognised Tom Chilton, yet that acute individual thoroughly made up his mind that the big man, who looked as if he had been up any number of consecutive nights,was none other than Mr. Ferdinand Stanhope, whom he had not Ken for more than two years, and who certainly had not improved in ap- pearance in the interval. (To leenntinuAd.)

FOREIGN NEWS.

The following circumstances, drawn from the •. Personal experience of Mr. Isaac W hick, of the * "Berough Arms," Dudley-street, Wednesbury, are k eo imbortant and really remarkable that they can- not help but be of interest andvalue to all readers:— . To the Editor. , Sun—My motives for the publication of the most len- ' • • usual statements which follow are, first, gratitude that . ...,I have been saved from a most horrible death, and secendly, a desire to warn all who read this statement against some of the most deceptive influences by which I tliey haveever been surrounded. It is afactthatto-daytheu- aands of people are within afoot of thegrave, and they do I • not know it. TO tell how I was caught away from just this position, and to warn others against nearing it, are I my objects in this communication. During 1882 I felt pains in the small of my back, Seadually growing in intensity until I was forced to cell • in my medical adviser. He diagnosed my case, and con- firmed my own ideas by stating- that I WES suffering from disease of the kidneys. He gave me many of the . usual remedies, put me on a strict diet, and for nearly three years I was under his treatment, but to pass water few ife stantly grew worse. I was forced ". minutes during the day t and night, and always th the e.r greatest pain and burning sensation. If allow to stand for a short time, a heavy white sediment would form in , the bottom of the vessel. Several times lily urine was . analysed beethe most competent men. I was frequently , confined to my bed for several weeks at a time, could not attend to my business, and had wasted away in flesh until I was a mere shadow of my former self. My ap- petite left me, and I began to consider my case a hope- Less one, as my friends showed by their actions that ' they did. In the early summer of 1885, after five years , et suffering and wasting away, an old physician to our family from a neighbouring city, was, at my re- quest, called in consultation with my regular medical attendant. A difference of opinion arose between them , as to whether my complaint was kidney trcrtible 1 or stone in the bladder, and a surgical examination was I decided upon, but could not then be m ' itee owing 1 to my reduced condition and the inflamed state of my bladder. In the meantime, though confined to my bed, it was decided to consult the most eminent reedieal man of Birmingham as soon as my condition would allow, In company with my medical men, all of whom reported large quantities of albumen as passing. from me, and all Weed that I was in a dangerous conaition. I went • to Birmingham, suffering greatly from the effects of the ' journey, and after a full examination and consultation, , was told by the physician no medicine would cure me. When I asked what was the matter with me, he stated that the acids 'passing through my bladder from the kidneys had entirely eaten away the inner lining of the bladder, and thatthiswas true hadbeen before provedby the analysis of my urine, in which particles of this lining had been found.- I 'then asked regarding my chances of recovery, but he said to me that my own medical man would tell me when we got home; , but this the latter refused to do, always putting me off with one excuse or another whenever I would ask him . what Sir had said about me. In September, 1885, I read a book left at my house, in which The symptoms of my disease were clearly put, and also some letters from people suffering as I was, and state- ments from them that Warner's Says Cure had effected Cures in their cases. I argued that all these people certainly could not lie and that, as I could get no bene- -fit from my medical men, I would try Warner's SAFE Cure. e bought one bottle, and after taking it, expe- rienced some benefit, my appetite iinprovee. and I was just a little better. I bought more, andwitlT each bottle I could see and feel an improvement., until, in January, 1887, I was so much improved that all my friends were amazed, and were congratulating me on my recovery. During part of this thee my regular attendant gave me naedieme which I put untested in the cupboard, and _..., continuedeaking only the Warner's Sees Cure, and con- stantly improving under its use. •It was now that my leledield man told mi that in the August previous Sir ""--- of Birmingham, had said I could not live three ementh.4, and at most not until Christmas (1885.) In all, !have taken only twelve bottles of Warner's SAFE Cure, the last some months ago, and during the time I took-no Other medicine of any kind; and to-day lam a perfectly evell mate and weigh seven pounds more than I ever did in my life, my weight now being thirteen storm and eleven pounds; my appetite is as good as it ever was, and I have no sign or symptoms of any disea.le or dis- order of any nature; and I consider that I owe my health Is not, indeed, my life to Warner's SA.4E Cure. , (Signed) ISAAC WHIM, Secretary of, Retail Brewers' Protection Association. A statement like the above needs no comment. .Those who are suffering should profit by the experience of Mr. Whick before it is too late. The remedy he used can be had of all chemists at 4s. 6d. per bottle, or of H. H. WARNER AND CO., 889 Clerkenwell-road, Lon- um, E.C. ,
ITALY.-TRE VATICAN AND IRELAND.-

THEFTS OF JUBILEE PRESENTS. Rows, SUNDAY Nront—ln• an article on that passage in the Queen's Speech referring to Ireland, the semi- official Moniteur de Rome claims that some of the credit for the diminution of crime in Ireland Is due to the pre- sence and mission of Mgr. Persico. The Moniteur ex- horts the Irish people to preserve a legal attitude, although it shows itself by no means in sympathy with the views of the British Government. The articie in a measure reflects the views entertained by the Vatican, Which, while deprecating any breach of the laws of the country, Iss in the negotiations with the Duke of Nor- folk, endea ,oured to obtain the modification of the ex- ceptional lilislation at present in force in Ireland. Rome, MONDAY Niour.—Archbishop Walsh, of Dublin, and the Bishop of Cork (Dr. T. O'Callaghan) were yester- day received by the Pope, to whom they =idea lengthy statement as to the situation in Ireland. The two pre- lates urged upon his Holiness the extreme inadvisability of doing anything to check the current of the Nationalist movement, pointing out the possible danger of any course tending to set the Irish people in opposition to the Vatican. The Pope replied that he hoped to obtain certain concessions from England on the Irish question Provided the Irish themselves adopted a legal and peace- ful attitude. The General of the Jesuits has presented £40,000 to • the Pope, being Peter's Pence from the Society of Jesus. The itatie says that various valuable objects have dis- appeared from the eNhibition at the Vatican, among Which are a chalice, worth nearly 0,000, many gold. snuff boxes, and several pairs of slippers. THE GERMAN C,ROWN PRINCE.- SAN REND, MONDAY.—The Crown Prince passed an excellent night. He sat up three hours yesterday There is no sign of fever or bronchitis. On Sunday, the Bishop of Derry, concluding his sermon in St. Bartholomew's Church, Dublin,' asked the prayers of the congregation for the Crown Prince of Germany, whose life, he said, was of the dmost importance to the Peace of Europe. Eminent not only as a warrior, but as a statesman, the Crown Prince was no less eminent for • his virtues in private life, as a husband and as a father. He was also one of the most beloved relatives of our gracious Queen, and at the cele- bration of her Majesty's Jubilee had received a most popular welcome. There was a particular reason why it was fitting he should ask an Irish congremition to pray for the Crown Princes recovery. An Irish lady, who was a member of the Church of Ireland, had been selected for her special training and knowledge to attend upon the Prince. VIENNA, TUESDAY.—A despatch from San Remo states that a cOnsultation of the Crown Prince's physicians took place this afternoon. the usual morning consulta- tion being deferred, owing to the patient being asleep. The prince passed a sleepless night, and it was not until this morning that he was able to get repose. There is nothing, however, to indicate any deterioration in his condition,there being no feverishness nor symptom of bronchitis. Sir Morel! MacKenzie is expected to leave to-morrow. • • AMERICA AND CANADA.—MR. BLAINE AND THE PRESIDENCY.—CHARGE OF TREASON.—ANOTHER DISASTER NEW YORK, MONDAY.—Mr. Blaine, who is now in Florence, has written from that city, announcing that he • does not wish his name to be presented to the Republican Convention, when that body assembles to nominate a, Candidate for the presidency. Oz-rawa„ MONDAY.—lntelligence received here from Victoria, British Columbia, states that in the Legislative Assembly on Friday last Mr. Humphrey charged the Ron. R. Dunsmuir, the Premier, with treason against Queen Victoria, on the ground that he was aiming at the annexation of Vancouver Island to the United States, and moved for the appointment of a Royal Corn-' mission to investigate the matter. The Premier denied the charge. Dupont's powder mill at Wapwallopen, in the Wyom- ing Valley, Pennsylvania, was blown up yesterday. It IS reported that 20 tons of powder 'exploded, blowing everything to fragments. Four men were killed outright and 40 more were injured-14 of them fatally. The Shock was felt throughcitit the Wyoming coalpits, and all the colliers hurried affrighted to the surface, fearing that some great disaster had occurred. Nearly every building in the town was either damaged or wrecked by the force of the explosion, and many persons there and in the vicinity were thrown to the ground. Glass was broken and chimneys fell at adjacent places, the explo- sion being felt for 20 miles round. . A telegram from Newo/ork. on Monday, announces that the ship firemen, from Stettin for,liew York, has arrived at Bermuda, damaged by contact with the logs from the great log raft. She was among the drifting logs for five days.

THE .FISHERIES CONVENTION. A Central News telegram, dated New York, Thursday morning, says :—The Fisheries Treaty between Great Britain, Canada, and the United States, was signed at Washington at seven o'clock last evening, by all the members of the Conference. Thbre is reason to believe that the provisions of the agreement, which are the re- sult of mutual concessions are satisfactory to the three , "ettunent4 con rued M Chamberlain will sail for ce . r.

England on the' 26th inst., and Sir Charles Tupper and Mr. Thompson will return to Ottawa to-day. COLLIERY EXPLOSION IN GERMANY. . FORTY MINERS KILLED. KAISEIMAIITERN, THURSDAY.—An explosion occurred last evening at the Ereuzgmben Coahnine, near Cam- phausen, in the Saar district, by which forty miners N*re killed. Thirty-six others were rescued.

div.p: IRETAND.
Constable Quigley, Government shorthand writer, Gweedore, has forwarded his resignation to the Inspec- tor-General, as a protest against the arrest of Father life.Fadden.
On Monday, near Fermanith, the police found the body of a farmer, named Carey, on the road side with his head and face battered almost beyond recognition. Another fnrmer has been arrested. _ . _

Bartley Geary, an old man of eighty, was evicted from his bolding at Kilkerrin, Connemara, on Thursday last. He retook possession of the house the same night, but next morning was found lying dead upon the floor. At a Crimes Act Court, at Derry, on Monday, seven persons were sentenced to three months' imprisonment for rioting, on the occasion of Father Mc.Fadden's arrest. Appeals were lodged, and the accused were liberated. Four men were engiged at Kilkee, county Clare, on Sunday, in towing a b&in of timber to shore, when their canoe upset, and two brothers named Shbehan, were drowned. The other two only reached shore with difficulty. At the Crimes Act -Court, Rathmore, County Cork, on Saturday, five men charged with unlawful assembling on the occasion of a seizure of cattle, were sentenced to, terms of imprisonment varying from a fortnight to a month. Peter O'Callaghan; for assaulting Sergeant Murphy, was sent to gaol for three months with hard labour. •

The Lenten pastoral of the Bishop of Cloyne says : Neither your duty as Christians nor subjects requires unresisting submission to a harsh and oppressive law framed to deprive you of your rights as free subjects of a free state. NA law, human or Divine, prohibits us from struggling against wrong by every means consistent with the law of God. AU that is required is avoidance of crizne and outrage condemned by Divinelaw. Not even the greatest god could justify means of this kind. An agrarian outrage was perpetrated at Kilcroliatri, West Cork, orNaturdav, in connection with which long sharp knives were, for the first time since the wurders in Phcenix Park, brought into use. The house of a man named Connor, caretaker, was broken into by 15, dis- guised moonlighters, armed with guns and knives. They demanded ConnoN revolver. He denied having one. whereupon one of the ruffians discharged his musket, but missed him. He was then brutally clubbed•with the guns, and his wife was badly cut in the hand as she seized a knife raised to stab him. Having warned Connor to quit the employment, they left. The depositions of Connor and his wife having been taken, the police arrested Michael Denis and Jeremiah M‘Carty, who have been identified.

THE POLICE AND THE IRISH MEMBERS. Mr. Fyne and Mr. Gilhooly have not,.it is announced, applied for the Chiltern hundreds. OniSaturday, Mr. Pyne, M.P., arrived at Kingstown, and proceeded to Dublin in custody. On arriving at Westland-row, he was placed in a cab and driven to Kingsbridge Station, another car following with detec- tives. He wall taken by train to Waterford. Thor.° was no demonstration in Dublin, few people being aware of his arrival. At Waterford he was formally charged un- der the Crimes Act, before Mr. • Bodkin, and remanded.

Mr. Gilhooly, M.P., who was arrested under such peculiar circumstances at Westminster, on Friday and who spent the night at 'the offices of the Detective Department in White- hall-place. was up early next morning, to be in readiness for his journey to Ireland. ' Mr. Lane, M.P.; was on Tuesday released from Tulle- more Gaol, after having undergone a month's imprison- ment,lo which he was sentenced at Riverstown, county Cork, under the Crimes Act, for making a speech at Watsrgrasshill, inciting tenants not to pay reht. During his imprisonment he has been several times put on " punishment " diet for refusing to clean hisceli

THE PROSECUTION OF THE MAYOR OF CORK. At Cork Police Office on Monday, charges preferred against the Mayor of Office, under the Crimes Act, for having on the 1-7th of January assaulted and obstructed a police sergeant 'named Knox while in the execu- tion of his duty', were heard before Messrs. .Gardiner and Warbuton, resident magistrates. The authorities adopted extraodinary • precautions to prevent any demonstration. Large bodies of police, armed with batons, revolvers, and rifles, guarded all approaches to the court-house, while coin- panics of the 4th Hussars and Scottish Rifles were drawn up outside. Bands were warned not to appear, but two serenaded the Mayor, and played through the city. Mr. O'Brien, on behalf of the Mac-or, admitted that. technically an assault had been committed, which should ordinarily be dealt with under the commonjaw, and not under the Crimes Act, and asked that that courseahould be adopted. Mr. Wright refused to do so, and said that Knox and other policemen interfered to prevent a League meeting, whereupon the Mayor caught hold of him by the collar of the coat and one of his arms, shoved him, and told him to go on his beat.
The Mayor was sentenced to 14 days' imprisonment without hard labour.
THE ARREST OF MR,BLIINT.-:-ACTION FOR £.5,000.

DAMAGES. , On Saturday, before Chief Baron ralles and 3 special jury of the City of Dublin, the hearing was comuienced of the action brought by Mr. Wilfrid Blunt against Mr. Byrne, resident magistrate, to recover £5,000 damages for alkault and false imprisonment in connection with his arrest at the Woodford' meeting on the 23rd October last. The defence was a traverse of the cause of action.* and also justification raised by special pleas. Mr. Walker, Q.C., Mr. Thos. MacDermott and Mr. Timothy Har- rington. M.P., were for the plaintiff. The Attorriery General, the Solicitor - General, M.P., Mr. Atkin- son; Q.C., and Mr. Carson for the defendant. The court was densely crowded, a jury box being set apart for ladies. Mr. Blunt was dressed in prison garb, over which he had his overcoat He wore ho muffler or Oiler, and he looked much thinner and paler than before his imprisonment. Be sat beside Lady Blunt in the side seat, where a warder stood near at hand: A large num- ber of police and- detectives were stationed in the court and its vicinity. The day was occupied by the mutt,. sel's opening statement, and the hearing of some unim- portant witnesses, On Monday, Lady Anne Blunt corroborated her husband's evidence is to the circumstances attending the suppression of the meeting. She said when he was pushed off the platform she put her arms around his waist. A policeman's baton passed close to her face, but did not strike her, and she was seized violently by the throat from behind, and her head pulled back,-and she was nearly strangled. All fell in a heap on the ground. When the police had been dragging her husband about for some time on the ground, witness called heaven to witness that they had killed him. A policeman twisted his arm. The speech of thA Attorney-General had not concluded when the Court adjourned. On Tuesday, a very large number of ladies were pre- sent. _ _ _

The Attorney-General, for Mr. Byrne, continued his address to the jtn-y. At the conclusion of counsel's speech there was some applause in court. Several policemen were then examined with reference to the midnight meeting. One sergeant was assaulted on the occasion, but after Mr. Roche had counselled them to 'patience, there was no further breach of the peace. Mr. Roche, and others, were subsequently prose- cuted and imprisoned. The court again adjourned.

On Wednesday the hearing of Mr. Blunt's action was continued before the Lord Chief Baron and a special jury. It was regarded as almost certain that the action would result in disagreement of the jury. . On Thursday, in the Blunt case, further evide,nce was given for the defence to show to what extent the prac- tice of boycotting was carried on in theWoodford district. Before the Court adjourned for the day one of the clergy attacked to the Roman Catholic Cathedral in Dublin wo called by Mr, Blunt's counsel to. show that, acoord- ing to the rules of the Church; a priest could' not cele- brate Mass in a private house without the permission of his bishop.

To TIIP: DEar.—A persona who was cored of deafness of 23 years' standing by a simple remedy will send a, description of it free to any person who applies to Nicholson, is. Camden Park-road, tendon, N.W.—Advt. Some excitement has been caused in the Slaideburn district, Clitheroe, by the appearance amon,gst the hills there of a large grey eagle. Some poultry has already been carried off by the bird. LIBERAL VICTORY AT DUHDICE.—The polling at Dundee was much quieter than had been expected. The result was declared shortly before eleven o'clock, as follows : Firth (Gladstonian) 7,856 Daly (Unionist) 4,217 The figures at the last election were :—Mr. Edmund Rob- inson (G L), 8,236 ; Mr. Lacaita (G L), 8,218; Mr:Nixon (L U), 3,545; General' Daly (L U), 3,346. The roll of 1886-7 contained the names of 17,093 Parliamentary elec- tors. The Parliamentary list, as made up last October, shows a falling off, as it only cOntains 16,613 names. HOUSE FURNISHING MADE EASY.—People who want to. furnish well and cheaply should obtain a prospectus and price list of the Globe Furnishing Company, of Pembroke- place, Liverpool, who have recently much extendedtheir premises to meet the requirements of an increasing trade. The mode of carrying on the business appears to com- bine the functions of dealer and banker, and, is an exten- sion to the general requirements in house furniture of the system which has long been successfully applied to the pianoforte trade. There is an impressio* that the hire-purchase system is a dear one to the purchaser, and in some cases this may be so ; but the prices put' forward by the Globe Company seem to be extremely moderate, and offer great convenience without ultimate sacrifice to people of limited means. COL SAIINDERSON, who was received with loud Unionist cheers, said the speech of the right bon. gentleman was a confession that he had entirely changed his ideas about the National League, but be did not give the House the grounds. (Hear, hear.) He objected to the action of the Government in Ireland because it was dangerous to interfere with the freedom of speech. Was that always his opinion Later on in his speech he quoted from the Kerry Sentiftel a resolution passed by the local branch of the National League, denouncing John Eitzmauricei who was afterwards murdered. • . Mr. E. HARRINGTON asked the hon. gentleman to read all the report, and there were loud cries of "Bead I" from the Irish benches. After other questions had been put the debate on Mr. Parnell's amendment was resumed by Mr. WILLIAM O'BRIEN, who eloquently maintained that the Irish cause was winning. The Government had failed to smash the Irish organisation, or to break the spirit of the Irish people, who had managed to survive the most horrible coercive Act ever directed against fiuman liberty. His criticism of the Irish Secretary whs scathing, and made a great impression upon the House. He pointed out the absullodity of imprisoning journalists, and said amid great laughter that Mr. Balfour might as well issue a proclamation suppressing the sun, and then go about smashing sundials for recording that the sun still existed. But one of his most effective points was that he had himself been treated worse than a thief and a robber for saving the people of his own constituency from a terrible fate—that of eviction. When Mr. O'Brien sat down tbere were prolonged cries for Mr. Balfour, but he did not respond, and Mr. R. div.head: PRIVILEGE.
div.p: PRIVILEGE.

At the end of the questions M. norm called atten- tion to the recent arrest of three Irish members, but the SPELICER held that in the case of Mr. Pyne and Mr. Gil- booty there was no privilege, and he confined his re- marks to the arrest of Mr. P. O'Brien, last Friday, in mistakcitor Mr. Gilhooly. He quoted precedents to show that it was egross breach of privilege to insult or inter- fere with a member of Parliament while going to or from the House and moved that the arrest, of Mr. O'Brien was a high infringement of the privileges of Parliament. _

_ Mr. BPLArcurr seconded the motion and was referring to the cases of Mr. Pyne and Mr. Gilrooly, for which ho was called to order. Be objected to the Government surrounding the House with detectives. Mr. H. Merraurws admitted that a most unfortunate and regrettable mistake had been made, but the police had apologised and he apologised on behalf of the Go- vernment. He submitted, therefore, that no further action was necessary, and thought that the Houle need take no further notice of the incident.

• Mr. P. O'Bruau gave his account of the circumstazices of the arrest, in which he denied that the officer ad- dressed him as Mr. Gilhooly, and complained that he was refused information as to the name a the superior official under whom the detective was acting. Mr. GLADSTONE, while admitting that a htindsome apology had been made to Mr. O'Brien, argued that the - conflict as regarded what happened on She occasion of the arrest necessitated its reference to the Committee of Privileges. He disputed the contention of Sir H. James, and insisted that in any case where the arrest of a per- son would justify an action at law such an arrest in the case of a member of Parliament became a breach of privilege. He suggested that the Government should accept an amendment to refer the case to the Committee of Privileges to consider whether any and what action should be taken, and to consider what measures should be adopted to prevent similar occurrences in the future. The SoucrroE-GESEBAL said the Government could not accept such an amendment, and agreed with Sir H. Jetties ibat privilege only applied to arrest on civil process.

Mr. PARNELL suggested that if Mr. O'Brien had been lan English member a different view would have been , taken of the matter.' He complained not only of the :arrest in question, but of the general conduct of Irish I detegtives to Irish members, although he paid a tribute Ito the civility of the metropolitan police. Mr. W. H. Slam, who, in reply to Mr. Haldane, denied • that the case of Lord Cochrane furnished a precedent for the present case, ridiculed the notion that the Com- mittee of Privileges could prevent mistakes in the future. Mr. Illingworth also spoke, and Mr. Picton's motion having been negatived without a division, Mr. Morley ' moved a further amendment on the basis of Mr. Glad- Stone's suggestion, but on a division the Attorney- 'General's motion was carried by 246 to 151.

THE ADDRESS.—MR. PARNELL'S AMENDMENT. The debate on the Address was then resumed by Mr. FLYNN, who tnaintathed that the Crimes Act, as was pre- dicted, had been used for the advantage of reek-renting landlords juid the extermination of tenants.—Mr. J. O'Cototosi denied that the Crimes Act had any share in the diminution of boycotting and outrage.—Mr. BLANE discussed the circumstances of his own case, contencling that his condemnation was illegal, and that the Act had been used, as in many other cases, fpr purposes of pri- vate vengeance.—Mr. O'llse complained of the prose- cution of Father M'Fadden. Mr. PARNELL, after justifying the opposition which was given to the passing of the Crimes Act last session. disclaimed any intention on the pelt of tho Irish mem- bers to obstruct the business of thcrHouse in the coming session; and, referring to the action of the Conservative party with regard to Ireland before the general election of 1885, he related the negotiations Whie,lT took place between himself and Lord Carnarvon, and asserted that their views on Home Rule then were identical. He next commented on Mr. Balfour's speech at Birmingham, which, he argued, was a direct incentive to his " removable " magistrates to 1:0..4 sentences which would prevent appeals; and, criticising his defence last week of the administration of the Crimes Act, denied the acculacy of the cases of boycotting he 9noted. Be attributed the decrease in crime to the patience of the Irish people • and having ciliated upon the success of the Plan of Campaign, asked why Mr. Blunt was imprisoned while Mr. Shaw-Lefevre was not interfered with. He severely blamed Mr. Balfour for proceeding against newsvenaors and foremen printers rather than against the proprietors of newspapers, and taunted him with having failed to suppress a single branch of the National League. He concluded by moving his amendment to the Address representing that the ameliorative legislation of last Session had tended to diminish crime, while the repressive legislation had done much to alienate the sympathy and respect of her Majesty's Irish subjects for the law, and that the ad- ministration of the Crimes Act, as well as much of the action of the Executive, had been harsh, partial, and mischievous.

The SOLICITOR-GENERAL for IRELAND argued that the improw‘ment in the condition of Ireland was due to the combined effect of the Crimes Act and the ameliorative legislation of last session. The debate was adjourned on the7rnotion of it G. TREVELYAN.
