TREVFILYAIq continued the debate on the Address. - He disclaimed having said outside the House, with respect to the Crimes Act, what, he was afraid to say in it. • A dozen times he had declared that the Act, and the manner in which it was administered, was one- sidad, misdirected, and out of sympathy with the great majority of the Irish people, that the Act 'had done little to suppress crime, and a great deal to alienate and shock public opinion; and he adhered to these state- ments. There was no sign that the Act was settling and pacifying the cotmtry, for it had only reduced outrages

div.head: ESCAPE OF. WOLVES IN LONDON.
div.p: ESCAPE OF. WOLVES IN LONDON.

On Saturday night, shortly after the termination of the pantomime at Sanger's Amphitheatre, Westminster, Bridge-road, an event which might have ended in a ter- rible calamity occurred. •In the morning a pack of eight wolves were received and secured in an iron-barred cage at the end of the stables. After the theatre had been closed and the lights put out a tremendous noise was made by the elephants, camels, horses, and birds of the menagerie, and the gasman discovered that the wolves had escaped. A search party, headed by the wolf tamer, proceeded cautiously down to the stables, where many of the horses were kicking and prancing, while some which had broken loose were careering madly about. The wolves *ere discovered ravenohsfy devouring the carcase of a horse which they had dragged to the ground. With some difficulty the halters of the horses that had not broken loose were cut and the ani- mals were got out of the stable, which was then barri- caded leaving the wolves and their victim inside. On Sunday morning when the tamer went to see how he could secure them he found that they had worried the greater part of the horse and were still extremely savage, and so postponed the operation. In an interview, on Monday, Mr. Geo. Sanger said he believed the wolves were let loose in his stables, on Saturday, by a malicious act of some evil-disposed person. On Saturday, his &tanager had occasion to dis- charge two grooms for misconduct, and these men were seen about the place just previous to the escape of the wolves; and it would be easy for a man to get on the top of the cage and lift the bars. no could then make an easy escapethrough the window, which is on a level with the cage-top. It has been ascertained that the men referred to left London immediately after the discovery took place, and that they are now in France. The wolves were secured on Monday afternoon in a new iron cage. On the tamer and his assistant appearing, the wolves growled ferociously, and one of the largest flew .at them. He was received with a heavy blow from the tamer's stick, and retired sullenly to the darkest corner. After this no attack was made by the savage brutes.

The trial of the Rev. Daniel Stephens, charged with inciting to criminal conspirary, was resumed on Wed- nesday at Falcaragh, County Donegal. The Court passed sentence of three months' imprisonment without hard labour. Notice of .appeal was given. FATAL ACCIDENT.—An accident, which unhappily re- sulted in the death of a little boy and serious injury to some other children, occurred on Thursday afternoon at St. Chad's Roman Catholic Schools, Cheetham. The thildren were leaving school when a stone staircase gave way without warning, precipitating those who were upon it to the floor beneath. A little girl (sister to the boy who was killed) and also a junior teacher tad frac- tured limbs. RAILWAYS AND TICE SNow.—The Berkshire and Hamp- shire railway, between Fewsey and Devizes, was opened I for traffic again at ten o'clock on Thursday morning after a two days' block. Two hundred men, with a snow plough and four steam engines, were engaged all night in cutting through immense snow-drifts. Hotels ' and waiting-rooms have been filled with weather-bound passengers. The mails to out-lying districts are being taken on horseback, but in many cases no letters can be delivered. Sapo-Lrvz," or Linseed Soap, cherishes the cuticle. 6d. post free. Kay Bros., Ld., Steekport.—Adot.
CURRENT POLITICS.

It is officially announced that Sir Michael Hicks- 13each has accepted the office of President of the Board Trade, in the place of Lord Stanley of Preston. The nomination of candidates for the representation of West Edinburgh has been fixed for Wednesday and ' the polling for Saturday. The nomination for the Don. caster Division of Yorkshire has been fixed for Friday next and the polling for Thursday, the 23rd inst,. Arrangements are being made to give Mr. Chamber-1 lain, M.P., a hearty welcome in Ireland on his return , from America. The right hon. gentleman has been in-, vited to address Unionist meetings in Cork and Dublin,, and it is confidently expected that he will consent to do so. At a meeting of the Liberals of Seuth Salford held on Monday in the Salford Town Hall, Mr. J. E. Barlow was unanimously and with marked cordiality adopted as the candidate in the Liberal interest at the next general' election. Mr. Barlow addressed the meeting at length on current political affairs. THE GOVERNMENT AND LICENSING. Mr. Ritchie, President of the Local Government Board, received on Saturday a deputation from the United King- , dom Alliance. A memorial was presented entreating the Government to accompany any change in the licensing system they might propose with a provision whereby the people in localities should be enabled upon this ques- tion to give a direct vote uncomplicated by any other issue, and that licences for the sale of intoxi- cating liquor might not then be issued or renewed in their midst contrary to their expressed wish. The presi- dent of the Local Government Board, in his reply, said the Government were in sympathy with the objects which the Alliance and similar organisations had in view. There was agreement as to the evils which resulted from Intemperance, and the desire to remedy them, but he doubted whether the agreement at the present time would go further. It was well known that one of the proposals of the Loe.l Government Board was to place the licensing of public-houses in the hands of an autho- riity other than the one which now exercised it, and, in adtlition to that, to give the authority the power of re- fusing to renew a license when it was Unnecessary. There .were, no doubt, more licenses in existence than were required. While he admitted the evils of intemper- ance, he warned them against resorting to what might be regarded as class legislation.

div.head: MR.. BRIGHT ON PEACE.
div.p: MR.. BRIGHT ON PEACE.

Sigrior Moneta, editor of the Secolo, of Milan, recently wrote a powerful letter in favour of Peace and Inter- national Arbitration which has received widespread attention. The London correspondent of the same journal, Signor Valera, having sent a copy to Mr. Bright, received the following in reply: "I observe with sorrow, if not with surprise, that tile Government of United Italy is treading in the steps of other Europeran Powers in maintaining large armaments, and in building great war-ships, furnished with guns of enormous magnitude, as if it had reason to suspect some ode or more of the Powers were about to attack the Italian" Kingdom. The tires levied on the Italian people are probably heavier than those levied on any other European nation, and taxes are wasted on armaments not needed for defence when no other nation dreams of making war on Italy. I should expect this weight of taxation would influence your people strongly in favour of peace. Your troubles now in the Red Sea are of your own making, and so long as Governments are allowed to commit such crimes T see no chance of redemption for the millions they represent, and whom they ought to protect."

div.head: TREATMENT OF IRISH MEMBERS.
div.p: THE TREATMENT OF IRISH MEMBERS.
RECEPTION QV MR. T. D. SULLIVAN, M.P.

Mr. T. D. Sullivan, M.P., left Chester on Saturday morning for Northampton. On Monday he went to London, and to-day visits Edinburgh. At Rugby he was met by Mr. Cobb, M.P., and a number of leading Liberals,who•drove with him to the Skating Rink, where he received deputations from the Liberal Associations of Rugby, Leicester Coventry, Banbury, Leamington, Southern, and other places.—Mr. Su/advert said that he and his colleagues went to prison not as enemies of Eng- land or the Union, but as the supporters of great reforms in the relations between the two countries. Be did no,t complain of 80. Balfour, because he believed his brutal and tyrannical conduct had done much to advance the effuse of Rome Rule. On reaching North- ampton the hon. gentleman was received by Mr. Richard Cleaver, J.P., Alderman Adams, J.P., and others, and drove to the Corn Exchange, followed by great crowds. The Mayor prpsided over a large meeting: Addresses from the Corporation and from several Liberal and Rsdical Associations were presented.—Mr. Sullivan said that such demonstrations as that would soon put an end to the brutal work of Mr. Balfour, who might as well be baying at the moon. The Irish members were prepared sacrifice even life itself, if necessary, in order to faci- litate reconciliation. Mr. Sullivan was warmly cheered. GREAT DEMONSTRATION IN LONDON.

Contingents from various parts of London marched on Monday to Euston Station, to welcome Mr. W. O'Brien and Mr. T. D. Sullivan, on their release from prison. The majority of the contingents started between 10 and 11 o'clock; but the muster was not large. The southern contingent, about 500 strong, reached the City at half. past eleven, headed by a band: while the processionists carried some banners. ‘ Remember Mitchelstown!" being the inscription chiefly in favour. Those following in this contingent were apparently of the better class of artisatis, well-dressed and perfectly orderly. The Cam- berwell and Peckham contingent reached the city in very scant numbers, shortly before noon, scarcely 200 persons marching in the procession. A band headed them, but , only two banners were carried, one of these bearing the inscription "Welcome free Speech," All those marching in this procession seemed to be of a respectable class, being warmly clad. Perfectgood order and good humour prevailed. The day was cold, but the sun occasionally shone brightly, and, so far as regarded the weather, the organisers could scarcely have been more favoured. By one o'clock, the hour at which the train bearing the ex-Lord Mayor of Dublin, was timed to arrive, there must have been 20.000 people in the vicinity of Ruston. A roaring trade was done by street hawkers of the Photographs of Gladstone, Parnell, and the heroes of the Plan of Campaign. Most of those who had come to welcome Mr. Sullivanand his colleagues belonged to the working classes, and a very large proportion wore green favours in their coats or hats. Only a privileged few were admitted to ' the plaiform, and these included Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P., Prof. Stuart, M.P., Sir Wilfrid Lawson, M.P.. Mr. W. H. Mclaren, M.P:, Mr. G. Howell, M.P., Mr. Pickersgill, M.P., Mr. Wm. Saunders, ex-M.P. for Hull, and several ladies, among whom WAS Mrs. Ashton Dilke, who wore a green dress. A large force of police was on duty to Prevent a' rush. and a number of platelayers, with red teulges round their arms, were in reserve. It had been I arranged that the carriage in which Mr. Sullivan tra- velled should arrive at a special platform, and shortly after one it steamed into the station. Messrs. Biggar, Carew, and Edward Harrington, k.P., who had first put in an appearance, joined the small crowd which pressed forward to shake hands with the ex-prisoner of Tullamore. Mr. Sullivan, who seemed in high spirits, entered a carriage with .Professor Stuart, Mr. E. Harrington, and M. Percy Bunting, and drove out into Seymour-street, where he reoeived a tremendous ovation, the people rushing after the carriage and almost completely blocking the street. The carriage, followed by a cheering crowd, drove through Ruston-road into Endsleigh Gardens, and a brief halt for lunch at Mr. Bunting's house was made. • The stoppage for luncheon caused a good deal of con- fusion, as the police along the route did not seem to be aware of the arrangement. The procession proper marched along Tottenham Court-road with bands and banners, and its magnitude may be estimated by the fact that it took nearly an hour to pass a given point. The crowd and processionists were in good humour, but the latter vigorously hooted as they passed Messrs. Maple's premises. There was an enormous crowd at tir Oxford-street end of Tottenham Court-road, and, although there was a large force of mounted and foot police on duty, a good deal of confusion pre- vailed. 'Several times coal waggons and omnibuses were permitted to break into the procession. At twenty Minutes to three the police, believing the pro- cession had finished:allowed the usual vehicular traffic to bee resumed. A quarter of an hour later about a dozen carriages, in one of which was Mr. Sullivan, drove along, but they made their way with the greatest diffi- culty, being in the midst of the ordinary traffic, and two miles behind the first part of the procession. In the afternoon, speaking to a vast assembly at the Reformers' Tree in Hyde Park, in acknowledgment of an address from the Liberal and Radical Federation and the Home Rule Union, Mr. Sullivan said that no words could express his feelings at the wonderful scene he had witnessed that day. The demonstration would be heard of throughout the world, and there was not an Irishman who would not feel grateful to the English people. He repudiated the idea that the Irish wanted separation from this country; but they did, he said, wish to be separated from the cruelty of the present Government. Among those who took a leading part in the proceedings were Professor Stuart, M.P., Mr. Pickersgill, M.P., who represented the Home Rule Union, Mr. Seagar, of the London Liberal and Radical Union, and Mr. Rneas Smith, of the Metropolitan Radical Federation. The demonstra- tion throughout was of the most, orderly character. Professor Stuart presided at a banquet which took place at the Criterion Restaurant, the guests of the even- ' ing being Mr. Sullivan and Mr. E. Harrington. The first toast proposed was that of "The Queen ;" and subse- quently the Chairman gave that of "The Guests of the the evening." Mr. Sullivan, in respouding, declared that Ireland would not be pacified by coercion, and expressed approval of the policy of Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Harrington also responded. The proceedings, were thoroughly unanimous.

Margarine smells as sweet under its own proper name as under that of butter. At any rate, our im- ports of margarine last month amounted to 119,812 cwt., showing an increase of 40 per cent, in comparison with the imports for January, 1886, while there is an in- crease of only 26 per cent, in the butter imports, which came to 138,213ewt. last month. So that in this case, as in many others, the effect of legislation upon the course of trade has by no means realised the anticipa- tions of people who believe in the omnipotence of Acts of Parliament.
GENERAL NEW. •
An Indian child, born in Buffalo Bill's Wild West caini; on the Manchester Racecourse, was baptised on Wednes- day in St. Clement's Church, Salford.

THE PIMP BISHOP Or WAKEFIRLD.—The RlOit Rev. W. W. How D.D., Bishop Suffragan, of Bedford, has been appointed to the Bishopric of Wakefield. The death is announced' of Mr. Seldon, C. 8., head of the Statistical Department of the Customs, who was the originator of what; are now known as the Board of Trade Returns. The Rev. Benjamin Wood, pastor of the Baptist Chapel at Bradford, sudd ly fell dead, whilst giving out a hymn at a prayer meeting, on Monday night. He had been pastor 28 years.. A THEATRE BURN-ED.—On Saturday night, the Theatre Royal at Blyth was destroyed by fire. The adjoining premises, the residence of the lessee, were also burned. The theatre only was insured. An action has been .begun by Mr. Hugh Watt, M.P., against Dr. Charles Cameron, M.P., one of the proprietors of , the Glasgow Daily Mail, for £lO,OOO for libel in con- nection with a charge of plagiarism brought against the former in a lecture, delivered about two weeks ago, on North Australia, in Lower Exeter Hall.

The Scottish News, a Conservative paper published in Glasgow, announced, on Saturday, that henceforth it would cease to appear as a morning paper and that here- after the proprietors would continue only their evening paper. It was the leading sporting morning paper in Scotland. There is now no morning Conservative paper in either Glasgow or Edinburgh. Tilley House, 'Wm, the residence of Mr. C. T. Dug. dale, was broken into between one and two on Monday morning, and the whole of the valuable plate, with other property, taken away. The thieves were undisturbed. It was generally believed that they were the same who broke into Tibstock Rectory, on Saturday morning, Wen being only seven miles distant.

Tnarr AT THE BRMSII MIISELTIL—The case of the Rev. Niblock Stuart, who was charged with mutilating a book at the British Museum, came before the Magistrate att How-street Police Court, on Monday. Mr. Stuart did not appear, and it was stated that he was in such a depressed condition of mind that he was scarcely responsible foo his actions. A fine cfive pounds was imposed. THE CAT FOR VIOLENT ASSATILT.It the Leeds Assizes, on Monday, three young men, na ed Geo. Greenwood, William Broadbent, and John Hamilton' were sentenced to six weeks' imprisonment, with hard labour, and 20 lashes with the " cat " for having violently assaulted, with intent to rob, a master miller "'named Belwood in one of the streets of Leeds shortly before midnight on February Ist. James Street was charged at the Birminghan Police Court, on Monday, with stealing £ll7 from a widow named Mary Few.—Prosecutrix lived the life of a miserly recluse in a small house in Grosvenor-street, being tip. parently without means of subsistence. During Satur- day night the house was broken into, and it is stated that the thief discovered £ll7 in gold and silver con- cealed in an iron pot hanging in the pantry.—Prisoner was remanded.

FATAL ATTACK ON A WORKHOUSE MATEOlL—lnforma. tion has reached Edinburgh that Mrs. Macleod, the matron of Long Island Poorhouse, in the Hebrides, has died from the injuries inflicted upon her by an inmate of the house named Currie, who, after savagely attacking the mater, stabbed the matron in the side and beat her about the head with a spade. Currie endeavoured to escape in a boat, but being driven back to shore by a storm was captured. DISTRESS IN SVOTLAND.—At a meeting held in Glasgow, on Monday afternoon, the Lord Provost presiding, it was resolved to establish a relief fund for the distress in the island of Lewis. It was stated that persons willing would be assisted to emigrate. Able-bodied persons requiring relief would have to work in making roads and harbours. Bailie Anderson and the Rev. Mr. Mc.Leod, from Storno- way, spoke of the destitution in Lewis. Liberal sub. scriptions were given at the meeting. DESTETYCTIVE FILCH AT MONTROSIL—Late on Saturday night Academy Flour Mill, Montrose, owned ,by Messrs. Mackenzie and Sons, with its contents, was totally destroyed by fire. From the inflammable nature of the building tile fire raged like a huge furnace for two hours, by which time, notwithstanding a fair water supply, the mill was a mass of ruins. The machinery was quite new. The loss, covered by insurance, is estimattd at from £lO,OOO to £12,000. The cause of the fire is unknown.

THB QD/OCN AND THIS BISHOP OF MANCHESTER.—We are informed that Dr. Moorhouse, Lord Bishop of Man- chester, had sometime ago made arrangements to preach at Walmersley Parish Church, near Ramsbottom, on the 4th of next month, but his lordship has stritten to the vicar, the Rev. J. D. Evans, intimating his inability to fulfil the engagement. as he has, since making the ap- pointment, received a command from the Queen requir- .mg his attendance at Windsor to preach before her Majesty on the same date. Critions DISPUTE nr JAPAN. - The Japanese papers report a curious dispute between a native railway company and a German firm which contracted to supply rail's. The company were informed when about to con- clude the contract that German rails were not only cheaper, but superior in quality to English rails. On their arrival It was discovered that the rails were all of British manufacture, and the company accordingly refused to take delivery. Ultimately the matter was compromised, but "German credit has been brought into great disrepute on account of the transaction."

SIMPOSED MeRDER AND rinlCTDP.—Early on Sunday morning, the bodieeof Emma Bradshaw, aged 27, wife of a labourer at Broadheath, near Altrincham, and her infant, aged 18 months, were found in the Bridgewater Canal. Bradshaw had been separated from her hqsband some time, and had a small allowance. It is supposed that she threw the child in its nightdress into the canal and then, stripping herself, itimped in after. From the circumstances it is supposed that the womari was driven to commit the act through poverty, as only a loaf was found in her house. She is said to have been quiet and industrious. The affair has caused a great sensation.

DitsrEners BURGIARS. The Barnsley magistrates on Monday co..imitted for trial two degpemte burglars named John Hardman and William Smith, both of Sheffield, for breaking into the dwelling, of John Green. wood, grocer, Broomhill, Wombwell, og Sunday evening, 22nd January: During the hearing it transpired that prisoners had been sentenced to repeated terms °film. prisonment, Hardman's convictions being 10 in number. The evidence showed that the police authorities—having received informatkon—secreted themselves in Green- wood's house and when the burglars entered at once threw themselves upon them. A desperate fight ensued, in which the burglars were seriously injured.

A LARGE ORDER IN Diserrit—The 'case of Macfadyen and Co. v. Milner and Co., which has occupied Mr. Justice Gfantham and a special jury at the Manchester Assizes the greater part of three days, was concluded on Monday. The action was brought to recover compen- sation for breach of contract to deliver 18,000 pieces of gray cloth. The breach was admitted, and the defen- dants had paid £225 into court in satisfaction of the plaintiffs' claim. The plaintiffs, however, claimed a much larger sum, and, in addition to the difference _between the market price of the goods at the time the contract was made and the time the cloth should have been delivered, asserted their right to a /min which they said would have to be paid to their Indian corres- pondents to whom the cloth was to be consigned. This claim, the Judge ruled, could not be sustained. In the result the jury fotind for the plaintiffs, awarding them £75 over and above the amount paid into court:

COMPANY—PROMOTING EXTRAORDINARY.—SOnIe extra- ordinary revelations as to the floating of local companies were made in the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, on Mon- tiay. The debtor was Philip Efebden Cowley, whose statement of affairs showed liabilities £12,368 and assets nil. The debtor had operated largely in converting the proprietary of vessels into limited liability companies, retaininc, the management himself. Re hal been connected with the Isle of Man Steam Naviga- tion Company, Limited, RS manager. He had also issued prospectuses regarding the Great Eastern to anchor the vessel at Douglas as a show ship, the capital to be £40,000 in £1 shares. In the course of examina- tion the debtor admitted that one David F. Houlstom who was to be secretary, and had taken one share, was the debtor's bookkeeper. and-was eighteen years of age, and received Iss. per week. In regard to all the com- panies the debtor had floated he had received from the public about £5,000, independent of the Isle of Man Company, and there had not been a penny of dividend paid to anyone. The debtor was ordered to file certain accounts, his examination being adjourned to the 26th March. ' EXTENSIVE ROBBERIES FROM TnE Li377inpoOr, POST OFFICE. —At the Liverpool Police Court, on Saturday, James Ktßothtwell, a well-dressed young man, was charged with stealing a golf: signet ring, a silver brace- let, and a number of silk pocket-handkerchiefs the pro- perty of the Postinaster-Geneml.—Mr. Crew, solicitor,' appeared on behslf of the Post Office authorities to prosecute, and Mr. Quilham was for the defence. The packet containing the ring was, on the 16th ult., posted by a lady in Woolton to a gentleman in the South of England, but it never reached its destination. The letter was not regis- tered, and was sent by the ordinary post. The loss was advertised, and a dentist practising in Park-road com- municated with the advertiser. He stated that he had purchased the ring as old gold from the prisoner, with whom he had some acquaintance, and to whom he gave a sovereign for it. Inquiries proved that the prisoner wag on duty. at the General Post Office when the Woolton post came in on the 16th of January. He was taken into, custody by Detective Allinson, to whom, in reply to the charge brought against him, he stated at first that he had bought the ring for a sovereign, but afterwards that he had stolen the letter containing the ring. At prisoner's house, 214, North Hill-street, there was found a large number of valuable artkles, eluding a diamond breastpin, diamond rings, gold wed. j ding rings, watches,ladies' and gentlemen's albert chains, l silk handkerchiefsotc. For nearly all of these things owners are now wanted by the authorities. The prisoner; was further charged with stealing, on the 21st nit, a silver bracelet, posted on that date at Seaforth by Edward Blundell, a rointsman on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway. In cross-examination it transpired that the prisoner was paid 245. 6d. per week: Be wag! committed to the assizes for trial.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 18, 1888.

.111 r. RITC-171IE; .M.P.; President of the Local Government Board, took sweet counsel the.. Other week with the representatives of the drink iraffics who are naturally anxious ;that they shall be as little interfered with as possible by the Local Government Bill which is to be brought before Parliament during the present session.' Mrßar• enis was too cautious to be drawn into preinature -revelations but he assured the gentlemen who addressed him that the Government, M any steps they took, would carefully coniider their interests. On Saturday the boot was on the other leg ;; the President of the Local Government Board,. was visited by a deputation from the United Kingdom -Alliance, who urged upon him the desirability of , providing in, the new , bill for the direct popular. control of licences. It is scarcely necessary to say that Mr. ,1144.ta took care not, to show hii,hand to these gentlemen, though he made it tolerably clear that neither he nor Lord SALISBURY viiis in favoullof the pi•oposals of the United Kingdom Alliance. He did, however, go the length of re- vealing the direction in which it isiproposed travel on the licensing,question. He said _ _

Of course it was of, no use to di§guise the fact that one of the_proposals in the Loot. Government Bill woutd certainly be a proposal to place the licen- sing of public-houses in the hands of an authority other than'the one which now exercised it, and that in addition to placing the existing powers,of the justices in the hands of that authority, powers would be confided to them which would enable them to refuse renewals of licenses when• they thought the licenses unnecessary. No man in this kingdom could shut his eyes tathe fact that there weie far more licenses in existence than were re- quired. /

This is, a grave admission, as coming from mem- ber of a Conservative Government, whose policy in the past has been to bolster up the trade;. ,and it • is to be hoped that legislation, when it is effected, will be fully abreast of this broad expression of . opinion. The fear which temperance reformers entertain, looking at the antecedents of the moo who are now in office, is that the bill will prove tO be one of large promise and poor performance. Mr. RITCHIE said : lie could not 611 the deputation what were the bodies which were to extrcise the power of licen- sing, or how they were Ifo be elected. The, Govern- ment would do their best to secure a lair and full expression of the opinion of the localities, and their view at present was, that having given the inhabi- tants pf the localities the power of expressing their views in a way now known/to the Constitution, no, would not be able to go much further in the direc- tion advocated by temperance reformers. It is pretty evident from this that the qc hange will not go to the root of the matter; and, if the bill should turn out to be unsatisfactery it will be for the House of Commons, and for the country, by putting pressure on the House of Commons, to amend it before it is placed upon the statute book. It is, of course, understood that the new authority will do the work sato granting or refusing licenses which is at present performed by magistrates; but what everybody is anxious, to know is whether the authority, such as it is, will be appointed solely for this work ; or whether the important matter of dealing with lidenses is to lumped, so to speak, with othe4 business which the newibody will be called.upon to transact. Another point of no small moment is whether magistrates who have to do with licensing as at present conducted, will be allowed to' have a footing in the new authority by virtue of their position as magistrates. There, is an uneasy feeling abroad that the Government may play the ex-officib trick; but if they do—if per- sons obtain a place in thb authority other than by election—it is not too much to say that the , measure. will belworthless, and will require to be reconstructed before it can possibly be acceptable to the nation. • Perhaps the most important issue which is likely to be raised in connection with licensing matters is the question of compensation for slicen- se s which are abolished. We do nofi ourselves see what legal claim brewers can have; and they cer- tainly have no moral claim to be paid an7thingc because the, renewal of a license may be-refused. But they are a powerful class, wealthy, and well- organised; and, having waXed fat out of the misery and degradation of their customers,' they will doubtless have the hardihood to, Suggest' that something should be given them if their power for mischief is resticied by reducing the nuniber of licensed houses. It seems to us that-the principle involved was determined when off-licenses -.were disestablished without a penny in the shape of cOmpensation. It would be a gross inequalitSr and a gross injustice to compensate the holders of full licenses whilst refusing compensation to holders of ofilicenses. It is rumoured that Mr, Rircinis will attenipt to overcome the difficulty which confronts him by, as one writer puts it, "making the trade pay for its own regulation." If; say a third of the licenses were abolished in any disttict, itis obvious that this action would add to the value of the re- maining two-thirds. Mr. Co-tram-Ey once 'sug- gested that the licenses canted might be put -up to 'auction, so that the money thus obtained might be used as.a means of compensating persons whose renewals had been i:efused,. This would be one way of making the trade pay for its own re- gnlation, and it would certainly have the advan- - tage of ispering the pockets of thapratepayers. Another way would be to raise the tax on the re- moiling licensed hopes to a monopoly figure, the surplus funds being ,'made use of as a conipene ition fund. In this way' Sir Prilbert anzrattrx might lose a score* of licenses, an 4 ob. , tairt compensation, but as • the. compensation
si it 3ted, ;ir of , rners mos re to Mr.

This means that Town Councils `- -shoi4a, by agreement or compulsion,possess'them- .. selves; on behalf of tile inhabitants, of all existing • :licensed.houses as" going concerns." They could therrreduce the liceni#4 at pleasure, seeing "that they-iiere dealing with their oweproPerty, withlregard to remaining licensed Itonses, the municipality wduld be the gainer to the extent of the profits that were made. . The, liCensilig bisi- "nem *Mild, in fact, be conducted by the Corpora- tion—just as they undertake the-siipply f 'graS or ' • water'---aiili,' as there Would be no. The aiffi-milty is that there are,large numbers of people who' haye = strong conscientious objectiens o havitig ?f.iiything to da with." the trade.;" and it is not to lie aeniefi, that the CrothenbUrg; sYstem involves Seridtis in its carrying opt, of jobbery and cori-uPtien. ?Ant there are difficulties whicheverytay-Wdrtkirri, especially when the question of compensation is ; • ; c!tkerr into account, and this is why, since- we are on the eve of legislation, the people require't,O be alert in order to protect themselves. There is no • _ . need to tell the brewers to watch their -own tercets ; they are always doing th‘at,' and... have hitherto hacl altogether too much control over 7 the House of Commons. A change is taking place which is for the bettea; let.us see'to it that I, it is fOr the best. _

• Tim imposing demonstration in London, on Monday, to welcome the lately imprisoned Irish members, and to express sympathjr with those who ' are even no* lying in gaol, will mark a red-letter day in the history of the Irish questiok; for it • places beyo,ncl dispute the fact that the democracy of both countries abe one in heart on ,the great issue which is agitating the kingdom 'lt was a happy thought to organise a welcome to " Balfour's criminals "—to let it be seen that those whom a dishonourable law has sought to degrade arc • honoured by the masses of this country as well as of /reland as men who have done nobly in freedom's cause. It is not for nothing • that from fifty to seventy thousand people assembled in Hyde Park on a wintry day, especially as those who attended had, for the most part, as Professor STUART re- marked, sacrificed a day's wages in order to be • present. There is a feeling throughout England, Which is gaining ground day by day, that the cause of Ireland is the cause of freedom; that the men* Who are being imprisoned for disregarding laws 'cinch basely trample on the sacred rights of free- dom of speech and freedom of the pritss are worthy •C.ff praise rather than blame. Take, the ease Of Mr. T. D. StrusvaN, the hero of the hour on Mondity. • Whilst occupying the exalted post of Lord Mayor of Dublin, he was sent to 00l for doing that Which, as a newspaper proprietor, it was his duty to do, Timely, supplying the readers of his journal with reports of National League meetings. He is a member of the National League;' his journal is pledged to advocate the Irish cause; and he would , have shown himself a traitor to his country and to

the freedom of the press if he had suppressed re- Ports of meetings at the bidding of Mr. BAfr POVn Mr. SumavAN is a gentleman and a scholar, a poet and a patriot, and the workmen of the metropolis did honour to themselves in honour- ing him and his colleagues on Monday last. Ancl how did he respond to the ovation? Was it with the voice of one who, whilst accepting the right hand, of fellowship, would strike a • deadly blow With the other? Let those who, heartless them- selves,. cannot trust the hearts of others, sneer as _ they will ; but the people of this country, as a whole, will believe Mr. ..SULLIVAN when he says The demonstration we have witnessed will 'be heard of by every Irishman living on the face of . the earth, and there is not one amongst them that will not feel grateful to you, and that will not feel growing up warm in ,his heart sentiments, not -merely of respect but of affection for this great peer ple—at all events, for the honest working masses solongst them— who, onceothey were shown and once they began to understand the real nature of our Irish demand, came to us in their thou- sands, aye,. in their millions, and pledged to us their faith, pledged to us' their word, that they would stand by us and assist us to achieve a rightful and just consummation of g. long and grievous struggle. kCheers.) As a representative Irishman, I wish to pledge So you the word and faith of my people that they mean to be, and will be glad to be, your friends, your allies, and your. brothers. for evermore. (Cheers.) " • All, this is better than the old mad notion that the people of Irel4nd are our natt6al enemies, and can ' be ruled only with a rod of iron., The Liberal party at any rate have grown out of that, and the little seed of kindness that has been sown has al- ready brought forth a hundred-fold. But the Tories, because they are Tories, do not 'learn; and Liberal Unionists are wis them because they are . of little faith. The Government are pursuing the ancient brutal plan; they are trying to keep Ire- land quiet by holding her down. And what is their success ? Net—absolutely nil. They cannot even drive discontent under the surface as of yore. .breaks out in every county in Ireland. Meetings are held nightly of branches of the League that are supposed to be suppressed; and, despite theterrors of Tullamore, they are reportedh every week in *yery Nationalist paper in Ireland. There is not An editor connected with one of these papers, is there is not a printer, there is not a newsagent or newsboy, who is not daily and hourly setting the law at defiance which declares that the publication of reports- of these tineetings is a criminal act. Th:, _ Government have cast their net,over the people of Ireland; but now that they have cast it they can- not draw it. They have sought to draw an, indict-. merit against a nation and they have failed. They have made a law so tyrannical that it cannot be enforced; it is broken everywhere under their yes. The prisons of Ireland' are too small and too few to hold the so-!called criminals. BAIXOUR. it;

beaten; voice and pen are proving mightier than the sword; 'force is shown to be no rethedy ; but there is hope in the heart of Irishmen that justice, ftnd kindliness, and truth, will filially ievail.'

It is .fiorno evidence that thing are a little bet- ter in Warrington than they were twelve months ago, that there are now WO inmate Of the Work- house, as against .11.0 last year at this time. Not being able to have an "At Home" at the Workhouse, they have gone abroad. Well, well, the master must do the best he can without them.

President Cleveland does not suffer in public estimation in consequence of his leaning towards a Free Trade Policy. Senator Blaine has been so far left behinds an opposing candidate for the next term of office, that he has felt under the necessity of withdrawing his nomination. The country will be none the worse for this. Senator Blaine is identified with all that is base and cor- rupt in United States politics. It is a tribute to virtue that he is driven from the field. '

Sir Michael Hicks-Beach re-enters the Cabinet as President of the Board of Trade. He made it clear to ..his constituents the other day that'he did not approve Oka the details of the policy of the Government; and it is significient that, concur- rent with his acceptance of office again, we have he announcement of a change in the administra- tion of the Coercion Act. It is understood that there are to be no more prosecutions of printers or newsagents. Sir Michael cannot stand that; the law is law, but it is not to be, enforced. , Poor Balfour 1 •

• At St. Barnabaa Quadrille Class, the other night, it is reported that the members engaged in "leap year dances," What are they, pray? Is it a case in which the lady saunters up to the gentle- man, begs to see his programme, and solicits the honour of a "square' or "round ?" And is it followed by the gentleman being escorted to the refreskment-roona, where sweet nothings are !mired into his ear while sweet vtrine is poured down his throat. And does it include his being lareaented with a pair of gloves, and being pro- vided with a cab? And, are there any other felicities—so that the brute in a black coat may wish it was always leap *par ? ,

St. lens has an unenviable reputation for fatal, and, as to many cases, preventible accidents. The inquest held as to the death of the Corpora- tion servant killed at the Obrporation Manure Depq shows that sufficient care was not taken to avoid accident. The poor fellow Riley was, along with others, pushing a waqgon away when the siding was run into by an engine driver, with the result that Riley yas crushed to death. It is true that the engine driver whistled; but, as the coron,er ,pertinently kemarked, with so many engines on the 'move at the siding, the whistle might mean tiny:- thing. The suggestion that the Railway Company should employ a man in the siding 'as a special look-out is a good one, and it is to 'be hoped the Company will, immediately carry it out.

At Widnee Petty Sessionsson Thursday, John Murphy, of 41, Crom- well-street, was brought up on remand charged with having, on the fourth' instant, done grievous bodily harm to Patrick Malone, of Marsh-street. The evidence showed that the men were employed as labourers at the works of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co., and on the night named, shortly before eleven &lock, they were in the Commercial Innewhich is situated ,on the Marsh. "Just for fun" it was said theenen had a "spar" to- gether in the inn, and when eleven o'clock arrived were turned out as usual. On arriving at the Works they had: an "argument," and shortly afterwards Malone hearing Mtiriehy ceilimlh. him from another part of the yard, went towards the spot, when Murphy struck him or threw at hitn a piece of Spanish ore. Malone admitted•athat at the time he was drunk, and the prisoner had some drink in him. Rendered unconscious by the blow, Malone Was taken to the time office by several fellow workmen; and Dr. Hutchinson•was called in. The doctor took such a serious•view of hie condition that he' was removed to the accident hospital, where he had remained up to that day. He had suffered frqm a contused wound which extended from the angle of the right eye up Wards to the left forehead. The wound as three inches long, and not onlypenetrated to the skull, but laid the bone quite bare. There was also a wound which penetrated to the bone, On the nose. Malone had lost an Immense quantity of blood, and for a week his life was in danger. A Hueco/us &DU/SELLER AND HIS CLOCIL. -- At Run- corn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. Henry Rey- nolds, Mr. James Reynolds, and Major Hazlehurst, Hy. Kelly, the landlord of the Holyhead Harbour Inn, High- street, was summoned for, keeping open his premises dunk, prohibited hours. -- P.C. 149 stated that at 20 minutes past eleven on the Bth Matz, he saw the front door open and a light in the place. He entered the house, and found William Fletcher with a pint of ale be- fore him. He asked the landlady if she knew what time it was; she replied that she did not; the. clock had stopped.—By Mr. Lake: The clock in the house stood at half-past ten. • Mr. Lake said there was no intention to committ an offence on the part of the defendant or his wife, who was managing the buSinesis that night. The clock had stopped, and the house was open by pure accident.—ln answer to the Bench Superinten up Hollmgsworth said there bad been no complaints ag t the.defendant. The defendant was cautioned and or- dered to pay a flne of is. and, coats.—William Fletcher, a boatman, of Northwich, was chO•ged With having been on the premises during prohibited hours.—P.C. 149 said that to the best,of .his knowledge the defenda,nt.was the man who had the pint of ale.—Eletcher stated that on, the night in question he finished unloading his fiat at the work% of Messrs. Gos.sage and Sim, at six o'clock. He went into Mersey-road. and purchased an• "Echo." and went back to the c.sbin to read it about eight o'clock. The defendant de- clared his intention of bringing an action for damages. Camden Mutual Improvement Class, Runcorn, under the presidency of Mr. Alfred Harrison, were entertained by a lecture delivered by Captain Le Couteur, entitled " A. sailor's yarn." The audience listened with great interest to the captain, who took for his hero the raw, country, lad, who had conceived the idea of going to sea through reading "Robinson Crusoe." , He detailed to them his various shipwrecks, the first on the coast of Holland when a boy, and subsequently another on the coast of Africa, which savoured of the Robinson Crusoe dreams of his youth, for they were rescued bye crew orfourteen, naked negroes, and dwelt ainong them -for five months, living chiefly. on goat's' fleCh, fish, and Indian corn, and tropical fruit ; and when he returned found his relatives in mourning for him. He told•thom that he was once five days in in open boat in the Atla- ntic, aiul finally stranded on the sandy barren island of St. Augustine, fifteep -miles from tiny habitation; but siinsequently met with the greatest hospitality from the prineipidinha'bitants of .St Augustine. At the close the captain wee awarded a hearty vote of ' thanka, which he duly acknowledged. This section has a length of. Sonie 'four miles, extend- ing from a point near Latchford to Irlame where • some important locks and sluices will be placed. Warburton is abbet mid-way between the two extreme points of the section. Woek began here a little.over twi inentles.ago,' and there are now 300 men busily. employed from day- light till darkness. 'The steam navvy is a comparatively new. feature on the greund. Two of these powerful ap- -pliances made their appearance a fortnight ago, and the excavation now goes merrihe forward. The cutting is already of Considerable' width -and depth. Inside the trench several lines of railway are laid, and a locomo- tive,•ealled the 41` Irlam,". puffs away all day, removing the full 'wagona excavated soil; and bringing up fresh supplies of empty wagons. • Above -the cutting again, and extendinvaboid a mile, is another line of rail- way, which will ultimately be carried to the extremity of the section.' Belo* the line of railway is a second cutting, In which another steam -navvy is tearing up the earth.with its strong iron jaws. A great increase will, no doubt, take place before long: It will then be necessary to build wooden hilts for the accommodation of the host of workers. In the meantime, however, the workpeopte find hospitality sufficient for all their needs. at Warbur- ton;Reatley, Cadislies,d, and Irlam. The line set out isabout a yard and ahalf on the Stretford side of the river, and at this point the Ship Canal will come to within a few yards of the htgh• way to Urm.ston, thus in all probability, the Rdman Catholic schools will have tb be interfered with when -a start is made: The sectiou extends from Salt Eye,eßar- ton, to Weaste. It is the intention of Mr. 'Walker; the contractor, to. proceed shortly with the erection of a num- ber of wooden hut§ for the use of the navvies who will be employed. ' At thelast meeting of the Barton Local Board plans were-passed for the erection of 43 houses in Ellen- mere-street,-and the surveyor to the Barton Rural • Sani- tary. Authority reported last -week that the number of plans passed by the authority during the past few -weeks had been greater than ally Other period during its history. At team the branch railway connecting the canal- works 'with the Cheshire Lines main line is progressing favour- ably towards completion. Upwards of 300 men are now employed on . the Irlam and CadishesA section of the canal. Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the' head office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning •

RUGBY RULES. FRODSHAM T. HALTON.— These teams met on the ground of the former on Saturday. Frodsham were very weak by the absence of Fletcher, Hayes, Hughes, and Molyneaux, forwards, and Rogers, batk. At the call of time, Halton had to retire beaten by three goals, four tries, and seven minors to nil. SUTTON V. WIDNES Racesseme.—This match was played at Sutton on Saturday, in grand weather. The ground being rather heavy greatly impeded the home backs, but nevertheless Sutton won by two goals, five tries, and seven minors to two minors. R. M'Cully (2), Grice (2), J. Fowles, Wilson and Twist (one each) scored the tries, Bickerstaffe and T. Fowles each placing a goal. Sutton had five tries disallowed. Rescone "A" TEAM V. ECCLES " A " TEAM—Played on the ground of the latter on Saturday. Runcorn was poorly represented, most of the ordinary players being Called uporl to assist the first team at Runcorn. Eccles, owing to the creditable performances they have made this season, thought they had an easy task, with Run- corn being placed at such a disadvantage, but owing to the reserve playing in such capital style were greatly surprised, Evans playing a grand game at half back, saving and passing in capital style. The forwards all played a good game, breaking away on several occasions with some fine dribbles almost the length of the field. Gatley, after a splendid rush by the visitors' forwards, - gained a try, Booth adding the premier point, Runcorn eventually winning by one goal and two minors to two minors. Sr. PAUL'S V. ST. HELENS (25D.)—Played at Warring- ton, before about 600 spectators. St. Paul's kicked off, and arbnce pressed, the visitors conceding a minor; shortly afterwards a combined dribble St. Paul's forwards ended in Johnson gaining a try, the kick at goal failing. From the kick out St. Helens dribbled into St. Paul's quarters; but not to be denied Mather got hold, and eluding the backs made a dashing run in, the kick again failing. St. Helens now worked the ball to half way, and from a scrimmage the ball was kicked acrosi to the St. Helens three-quarter, but Gardiner dashed up, and gaining possession made a grand dodgy run in Mather kicking a goal from the place. Half-time was called with the score : St. Paul's one goal, two tries, two minors, to nil. St. Helens restarted and slightly pressed, but the back play nf St. Paul's being too good, the ball was soon in St. Helens quarters,. where Lawless got hold, and overcoming all opposition got in close to touch, no goal resulting, Noon restarted on behalf of St. Helens, but they could not relieve their lines, St. Paul's scoring four minors in quick succession. Time was now called with play on the St. Helens lines, the ' score being—St. Paul's, one goal, three tries, six minors; St. Helens, nil. BRADFORD V. ROSCOLOC—This match was arranged to take place at Bradford for the benefit of the Chari- ties, in lieu,of the Liversedge V. Buttershaw Charity tie, which had fallen through. The ground had been covered with straw, and was in fair condition. Runcorn brought a representative team. Bradford played several strangers as substitutes, including Eastwood and Dunlavy (of, Brighouse), and Holmes and Pighills (of Manningham), but had a very good team. About five thousand specta- tors were present. The visitors played with the wind in the first half, and though they conceded a minor, they then pressed Bradford hard, and were rewarded by Broadley getting a smart try. from which Wood landed a goal. On crossing over, Bradford had conpiderably the best of the game, though Speakman, Wainwright, the brothers Hughes, and Wood repeatedly did some clever work. After several minors had been put Hawcridge took a drop at goal, which Jowett followed up and made into a try, but his shot, from a difficult place, went outside. Soon afterwards .Herbert Robertahaw, who was playing once more, got a try by one of his old irresistable rushes. This point was under the post, but Eastwood's kick missed the mark. In the last ten minutes a Runcorn man threw the ball forward, and Eastwood, getting hold, by a fast run got a try under the posts, from which he kicked a goal, and thus gave vic- tory to Bradford The Runcorn team, expecting the ball to be "ruled back," were standing still whilst this point was made. Score: Bradford, 1 goal, 2 tries, and 5 minors; Runcorn, 1 goal. WIDNES v. MANCHESTER RANGERS.—Teams from these organizations Filet at Widnes on Saturday, before about 1,500 spectators, to play off the return fixture. Two "third" were decided upon, and the Rangers winning the toss, and deciding to play down the slope, Smith kicked off. For some time play Continued without any point being scored, Widnes pressing, until at last Farrell passed nicely to Parkinson when in the visitors' quar- ter, and that player made a brilliant drop at goal, the ball just missing. It was afterwards kicked dell. Fpl- lowing the drop out the visitors rushed the ball up the field, and Bingham had to touch down. Subsequent play tranferred the leather to the visitors' territory, whence a fine dribble, headed by Smith, Plumpton, and Gandy, took the ball over the line, Plumpton scoring. A good attempt at goal was made by Farrell, but the major point was not scored. Half-time was shortly afterward called. Soon after the change of ends, Parkinson passed to Plumpton, who gained a meritorious try near the cor- ner flag by a splendid run half the length of the field, and right past the majority of his opponents. Son after the same player dropped a goal. Ratcliffe got over for the visitors after a neat dribble and the whistle soon after sounded for time, with the ball in the centre of the field. All the home team played well, Plumpton being worthy of special mention. Sabin *as by far the best man on the losing side, but he was too well watched by Farrell to do any harm. Of the others Ratcliffe, Parlane, Herbert, Hasleham, and Mee were the pick. Teams : Widnes : S. Bingham, back; Plumpton, Farrell, and Parkinson, three-quarter backs; Wilkinson and Barker, half backs; Smith (captain). Kiddie, Hardman, J. Bing- ham, Pennington, Gandy, Woods, Barber, and Hughes, forwards. Rangers: Jones, back • Sabin, Alfred Ham- nett, and Ratcliffe three-quarter 13.4,cks • Parlane and R. Hamnett, half backs; H. Hasleham (Captain), Frost, Mee, Pollard, Common, Scrowley, Barrow, McDougall, and another, forwards. WYCLIFFE V. GRAMMAR Scwoot, (ler TEAMS).—The return match between these clubs was played on the ground of the latter, on Saturday, in cold weather, in the pxesence of about 500 spectators. Neither team was fully represented. Webster having won the toss, J. Knowles started the ball on behalf of Wycliffe, and the ball not being returned a scrimmage was formed in the home 25. The visiting forwards dribbled over the line, the home saving. This they had to repeat twice in rapid succession. Webster dropped out, the ball laeing well returned by Sampson, and good following up off the part of Wycliffe forwards resulted in S. Pickton getting a- try close to touch. J. Knowles made a good but un- successful attempt at goal. Soon after this W. Knowla passed nicely to Scott at half way, who rounded all his opponents in fine style, and gained try number two. J. Knowles again took the place, but failed. Wycliffe con- tinued to have the best of the play, and, after a nice dribble, Hayes got try number three, Sampson failine at goal. Nothing of interest occurred from now up to half time, with the exception of three more minors for 41 Wycliffe. Score at half time—Wycliffe three tries, six minors; School, nil. Webster restarted, and Sampson returning well, play was taken slightly into the home quarters. From a scrimmage here, the Wycliffe forwards again took play to the line, the home team saving. Lally dropped out, the ball being well returned, and Thornton being collared with the ball, caused a scrimmage close to the line. W. Knowles passed nicely to Hamer, who crossed the line in a favourable position, but Sampson again failed to land a goal. The home team fell off con- siderably after this, Wycliffe doing just as they liked. From a scrimmage at the home 25 W. Knowles again - passed nicely to Scott, who ran in behind the posts, Hayes landing a goal. Webster restarted from centre with a hugh kick, the ball going dead. J. Knowles , dropped out, and Webster, after a nice run, got a try, Whittle kicking a goal: This seemed to rouse the home team, and they played up much better. Soon after this the whistle sounded for "no side," leaving Wycliffe the winners of a pleasant game by one goal, four tries, eight minors, to Grammer School one goal, one minor. For Wycliffe, Sampson at full back played a splendid °Arne all through, as did also W. Knowles, Hamer, and J. Knowles, whilst for the School, Webster, Kidd, and Lally were best. Mr. W. Speakinfin (of the Warrington F.C.) officiated as referee, and gave general satisfaction. RUNCORN V. LES.—Played at Runcorn, on Satur- day. Owing to the inclement state of the weather, the attendance was not so large as usthil. The match was also deprived of much interest owing to the Cheshire and Yorkshire match at Birkenhead, seven being chosen to represent their county, which caused the home team to -call very heavily on the "A team," who showed by their form on Saturday that they could be fully relied on in C.:l-sf. of emergency. The match was an uninteresting one, Eccles playing the old'-fashioned game of packed scrimmages. Brazendale again played well at full back, i putting n some tremendous kicks. Davies played very well in the first half, and made strenuous efforts to score, but the heavy state of the ground was much against his style of play. Woods was very tricky at centre, and Andrews and Whitby played well at half. Amongst the forwards Stubbs, P. Riley, Dolan, and Gayter showed up very prominently for Runcorn. Efferson, Halsall, Ruebottom, and Lythgoe were the pick of Eccless, but their halves played very much offside, which greatly in- terfered with the back play of the home team. Runcorn won the toss, Eccles kicking off, Woods returning to cen- tre. The visitors soon forced play in the honae 25. Davies relieved with a nice run, Woods passing to Riley, who took the ball on to centre. Dolan intercepted a pass intended for Efferson, passed to Woods, who trans- ferred to Davies, the latter almost getting in after a good run. Eccles relieved, and some nice passing ensued be- I tween Woods and Riley. After some even play at centre, Woods got a free kick. which gained considerable ground, Moores relieving with a timely kick. Woods getting his kick charged down, Lythgoe secured the ball, and passing to Ruebottom, the latter player got an easy try between the posts, a miserable attempt at goal being made. Soon after the kick out the home forwards with a ,eeneral rush forced the visitors to concede another minor. After the kick out, Whitby passed to Woods, who took a drop at goal, the ball passing just outside the posts. After some even play at centre, H. Andrews made a good run, and passed to W. Riley, who took play into

div.p: tlie visitors' quarter, and after some loose play close to the line, again got possession and secured a try close to ,the corner flag, Bmzendale making a splendid attempt at goal. The whistle sounded for half-time shortly after- wards. Runcorn kicked off and quickly forced play in the visitors' quarter, where some heavy scrimmages took place, from which P. Riley broke away with a good dribble, scoring the second try for Runcorn, Brazendale failing to add the major point. The home forwards, Leaded by Dolan, Abrams, Gayter, and Hancock, took the ball in an excellent combined dribble over the visitors' lines, when a lengthy maul ended in a touch- down. The game at this period was somewhat marred by very heavy showers of hail. Shortly afterwards Woods was compelled to concede a minor. Scrimmages were now the order of the day, nothing of any note transpiring, owing to the visitors continually lying on the ball. The game eventually ended in a win for the home team by two tries and fl' minors to one try and 'one minor. Teams :—Eccles: Full back, Loots; three- quarters, Moores, Effsrson, and Daisy: half backs, Hal- sail and Drury ; forwards, Chambers, Nunn, Pickup, Rue- botham Haseldon, Worthington (captain), Davies, Lyth- goe, and Blakely. Runcorn: Full back, Brazendale ; three-quarters, Davies, Wood (captain), and Riley; half backs, Whitby and H. Andrews; forwards, 'Han- cock, Stubbs, Gayter, P. Rijey, Raffe, Dolan, Cox, Andrews, and Abrams. WARRLNGTON V. HALIFAX.

The third visit of the West Lancashire organization into the comity of many acres took place on Saturday, when Halifax were encountered for the first time An early start was made by the Warriagtonians, and the team arrived in Halifax at two o'clock. A 'bus being placed at their disposal, the journey was made up to the ground, which was reached after a oomewhat tedious and cold drive. On arrival a minute inspection was made of the Hansom-lane ground. It is fitted with all the latest improvements, including electric light, and to ensure that the match should tale place, the ground had been covered with straw. It may safely be termed the model football ground of Yorkshire. Soon after three o'clock both teams made their appearance in the enclosure, and it was noticeable that Dodd and Buckley were absent from the ranks of the Halifax team, whilst Speakman and Dillon were away from Warrington, the latter being absent through indisposition. '

Barnes won the toss, and elected to play with the sun in his eyes. Allbutt kicked off, and the ball being charged down, Ashton dribbled to the Halifax quarter flag, WeLsfisaving the rush. The latter got the leather away to Massey, only to see the Warringtonian return as promptly in touch close to the Halifax line. The home team relieved to half-way, and Nevins was applauded for some sterling work, relieving his side from his own quarter flag to that of the opposition: Welsh was awar- ded a free kick, and similar fav9prs were shown to "Morris," but neither gained any material advantage. Pretty exchanges were now witnessed by Barnes and Sharinan but Warren, assisted by Fair. Turner, took the game well into Yorkshire territory. From a pack at 'quarter flag, "Morris" passed neatly to Barnes, who, evading a few of the opposing backs, was collared close to the line, but transferred to Jolley, the latter being held on the line, just when on the point of grounding. The leather was brought out of danger by Creenwood and Baldwin, and Lord helped this advantage by a neat run and kick to half-way. Webh responded to a kick by "Morris," and a return being made by Nevins, Barrett with a huge punt scored the first *minor to Halifax. From the drop out Barnes intercepted a pass intended for Sharman, and relieved the slight pressure to half- way. Play of an even nature was now witnessed, and from a pack in the Warrington quarter an invasion was made into the Halifax quarters, but it was only tem- porary, for Greenwood and Scholefleld, by judicious kicking, placed Warrington on the defensive. Lord passed well, but the safe tackling of the visiting backs did not allow of any liberties being taken, and play was again confined to neutral ground, and from long kicks the home team scored two dead balls. Grand passing by the Warringtonians was now witnessed, and Nevins was to the fore by a smart kick to the Halifax quarter flag. Warren compelled he Halifax team to act on the defensive, and from some neat play which followed Fair. Turner got in a neat run and pass to Jolley, the latter being safely held by Baldwin. Clowes was awarded a . free kick, but the visiting team, who were playing splendidly, forced the Yorkshiremen back, and rushed the leather down the field, and for a few moments the Halifax goal was placed in jeopardy. Relief was brought about by a neat dribble by Pewee and Wilkinson, but Warren neutralized the advantage gained by a smart run and pass to Massey. This brought about about half- time, with the score as follows—Halifax three minors, Warrington nil. Frank Turner re-Started from centre, and a rush by the home team settled play fn the War- rington quarter flag, Massey saving in daring style. From a line-out at the quarter flag the ball was taken dangerously near toe Warrington line, and from a pack here •'" Morris" in trying to relieve his side had his kick charged down by Lord, which enabled him to score an easy try. No goal resulted from the place kick. Frank Turner re-started, and Povey was instrumental in reach- ing the Halifax quarter flag. Clowes dribbled back, Nevins stopping him, and Greenwood by a smart kick placed the gafne in the Warrington 25. The game was of a very fast nature, and from some loose play in the Warrington territory. Jolley secured possession and made the run of the day, dodging to perfection, and only being brought down at the Yorkshire quarter flag. From a line-out here the visiting forwards rushed the leather down the field, only to find a stumblirigblock in Welsh. Greenwood again placed his side on the aggressive, and the Warringtonians were forced to find relief by conced- ing a &nor. Exchange kicking by Massey and Shar- man was witnessed, and Barnes but in some brilliant work frote his own line to half-way, tackling Greenwood before he could get the leather away. This proved to be his last share in the game, as an unfortunate accident had happened to him. He Had to be assisted off the field, when it was found that a severe sprain of the ankle had caused his retirement. Massey took his place at centre, and Bandies went three-quarter. The ganef, was proceeded with, and sterling work by JVlley was applauded. The Warringtonians, considering they werd short-handed, played up in marvellous fashion. Warren effected a grand run, but the pass was wide. Turner placed the home team on the defensive, "but the York- sire forwards again came away, Watson almost getting in. Davies relieved his lines gallantly, but a long kick by Lord ended in another minor being credited to the home team. The drop-out found play at centre, and Massey with a huge punt to Barrett enabled Ashton to safety hold him liefore he could part with the oval. The home team now showed up with a combined dribble, compelling Nevins to save. Similar tactics were resorted to shortly after, and from some loose play which followed Sharman dropped a goal in fine style. From the re-start- ing at centre Sharman passed badly to Halliday, and Littlewood racing up took possession and dashed over the line. Fair. Turner failed at coal. The Visitors played grandly, but could not add to their score, and in the end Halifax won a grand game by one goal; one try, nine minors, to Warrington one try. The game was of a fast description, each side showing to perfection in each department, the tacking, running' dribbling, and kicking earning for the players rounds of applause. Nevins played splendidly at full back, and improved greatly on his performance of the previous week. Saturday's match was the finest exhibition he has shown in this position. Barnes was playing a splendid game until he got hurt, and to this misfortune must be attributed Warrington's defeat. He never al- lowed the opposing centre to gain a yard, whilst he puzzedthe Halifax team time after time with his tricky play. Both Jolley and Massey played well, the strong runs of the former gaining him plenty of admirers. Both halves played a grand game, passing with precision. and Warren showing to perfection. All the forwards played with untiring energy, and when Barnes got hurt it seemed to infuel fresh life into them' and they worked in splendid fashion to make up for the deficiency. To make special mention in this division weiuldbc an injustice On behalf of Halifax, Greenwood, Scholefield, Wilkihson, Clowes, and Baldwin were the best. The following were the teams I,—Warrington : Full back, W. Nevins; threequarter backs, J. Jolley, T. Barnes (captain), and J. T. Massey; halfbacks, J. E. Varren and " Morris " forwards, H. Ashton Fair. Turner, Frank Turner, T. Davies, LittlewOod, W. Randles' W. Hayes, W. Povey, R. Eyes. Halifax: Full back, W. Barrett; threequarter backs D. Welsbv, J. Sharman, and T. W. Greenwood; half backs, G. Schole- field and M. Lord; forwards, G. Miller, J. Stansfield, F. Halliday, J. P. Clowes, W. Baldwin, J. Webster, F. G. ' Buell, H. Wilkinson, and T. Allbutt (captain.) Referee, Mr. H. Hayley, Wakefield, F.C.

• NOTES BY - THE WAY. The votaries of football in Runcorn had quite a day of rejoicing on Saturday. The local club contributed seven of its best men to the Cheshire county team that so' smartly defeated Yorkshire the first team with these good players absent, proved fully equal to defeating Eccles at Runcorn, and a scratch team sent to the town of cakes to meet the "A " team, also came back con- querors. Wainwright was the hero of the county match, scoring a try after one of the most brilliant forward rushes ever witnessed on a football field. He had also another good opportunity of . scoring, but through his usual fault of strong kicking', what appeared to be a cer- tain try was lost. With the exception of Cawley, who was out of form, the Runcorn representatives did a lot of clever work. The match Widnes V. Manchester Rangers was 're- markable that the whole of the major points scored by the Chemicals were credited to Plumpton. For some weeks past he has been playing in brilliant style, and he fairly excelled himself on Saturday by dropyfing a goal and getting two tries. After the long series of suc- cesses by Widnes is it necessark to say that the Rangers returned home well-beaten? Runcorn journeyed to Bradford on Tuesday to meet the club .of that name, and although defeated were not disgraced. It is said that the game was one of the fas- test and smartest exhibitions seen on the ground, and both the home team and the visitors were frequently cheered by the five thousand persons assembled. Vic- tory was snatched from Runcorn in a manner that is most aggravating to the Cheshire champions. Within a

few minutes of time,. HUghie made a pass forward, and a Bradford manobtaining possession, quickly made to- wards the goal line. Under the impression that there had been an appeal, and that the ball would be ruled back, the wearers of the green quietly watched the player's progression over the line, but judgrof their dis- gust and indignation when Captain Jtushworth, the re- feree, allowed the try, and a goal was kicked from the place. Up to that point Runcorn were leading. For- tune did not favourthe visitors, for Faulkner planted the ball over the line after some good play, but the point was disallowed, and " Pat" Woods, after threading his way through the whole of his opponents and running the length of the field, lost his head,, figuratively speak- ing when he was approaching the line, and -foolishly parted with the ball, and a certain try was thus boat. The cry already is " Wait until Bradford visit Cheshire, and the defeat shall be wiped out." On Saturday, Warrington visited Halifarx to.encounter another of the powerful Yorkshire combinations) and, after a capital contest, .returned defeated by a goal, a try, and nine minors to a try. In the latter part of the game the visitots were handicapped by losing Barnes through an unfortunate accident to his ankle. This, it is needless to say, dieakened them very considerably for either aggressive or defensive purposes, but nevertheless they played up pluckily, and made a good game of it. The return match with Halifax, which, however, is not to come off till the 7th April, will be one, of the most in• - teresting played in Warrington this season.
THE SHIP CANAL WORKS,
AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.
NO, 5.-DEVIATION OF WARRINGTON
AND ALTRINCHAM RAILVOAY..

In the first three articles of this series, we—by what Professor Tyndall describes as a scientifl,6 use of the imagination—gave a portrayal of the changes which will be wrought by the soaking of the Ship Canal in Arpley Fields, around Lower Walton, and in the neighbourhood of Stockton Heath. In the present article, we propose to fore- shadow further changes which will even more closely affect Warrington than' most of those already referred to, and in doing so we will still base all our forecasts and prognostications upon a careful study of authentic plans,. Acts of Parlia- ment, and. other sources. of,the needful informa- tion.

and some distance beyond Latchford station. This deviation will commence somewhere, about thirty yards to the east of the level crgesing over Wilders- pool-causeway, at a place where the yard and ground in the occupation of Mr. Voe. LawTiaton ad- join the present railway. The deviation will be made on blie northern side of the existing line Of rails, that is to say on the side nearest Kuutghard- road. The new line will be laid on embankments which will gradually raise it by a gradient of one in 135 until it reaches he point beyond Liftchford sta- tion at which it crosses the Ship Canal, when it will begin to fall by the same gradient until it reaches the present level of the railway on the nearer side of Thelwall station at the point almost opposite Thal- well vicarage, the residence of the Rev. T. Pym Williamson. The whole length of new railway to be constructed is two miles, four furlongs, and be- tween two and three chains. From the point of commencement near the Wilderspool level crossing, the new embankment will skirt the Old one very closely, so closely, indeed, that it will pass between the house occupied by Mr P. Caldwell and the existing embankment, though the limits of devia- tion, that is to say, the limits within which the Canal Compan.y have power to obtain land and , other property by compulsory purohase, include Mr. Caldwell's house and extend some distance out- wards. The new railroad will continue to " hug " the old one till opposite Howley it crosses the Run- corn and Latchford canal, which, as we mentioned last week, is to be preserved between Stockton Heath and the Mersey. Once across the canal, however by the new bridge that will be made to aCcommodate It, the course of the new railway will diverge some- what more widely from the present lines of metals. At the Latchford canal the limits of deviation ex- tend between 100 and 200 yards towards Black Bear Bridge and include part of the occupation road, and public footpath which lead from Wash-lane over the canal, and doubtless the new cottages that stand near the eastern bankof the anal within the limits, but which, haying only recently been built, are not shown on the plans. Once over the Latchford canal, the new railway strikes in, a pretty straight line across the fields in which the new siding has been laid down from Latchford Station to tips banks of the canal; and it intersects Wash-lane abOut fifty yards nearer Christ Church than the present rail- way ; in fact the new embankment will be laid over the site of the two cottages on the eastern side of Wash-lane, at present occupied by Mr. R. Board- man and Mr. W. Llollinsworth. The limits of devi- ation at this point include on the one side, the farmhouse, outbuildings, &c., in the occupation of the executors of the late Mr. John Hall, and also the holse, gardens, and conservatories occupied by Mr. W. Pierpoint. as wtall as the short occupa- tion road which ,branches off from the left of Wash- lane up to the goods yard at Latchferd Station. On the southern side the limits of deviation extencl, through most of the length, only a few yards from the present railway. At Wash-lane they do nf,t in- clude the Baptist Chapel, which is in close proxim- ity to the existing line, but they do include the roadway, which branches off to the east from Wash-lane crossing, and also the two houses standing on this roadway, belonging to Mr. Frederick Jenkins. Continuing along the new-rail- way, it is found that it crosses the road leading from Knutsford-road to Latchford Station, at a• distance of about forty yards nearer Knutsford- road than the present level crossing, and at this point the new station for Latchford will be con- structed. Theelimits of deviation do not here seem to include any of the existing residences. Still pursuing its eastward course, the new railway will run over the site of the house, coachhouses, &c, on the right of IPultBford-road, occupied by Mr. Lonsdale, but this. is the only residence that is included in the limits of deviation at this particular point. From Knutsford road the new railway will run through the fields parallel with the old one, at a distance away of about fifty or sixty yards until it reaches Cross-lane, a roadway connecting Knuts- ford-road with Thelwall-road, when the two lines will be separated by a somewhat greater distance. Cross-lane is to be stopped as a thoroughfare, and the limits ofeLleviation here include farm buildings in the occupation of Mr. Stephen Howson, and other houses, gardens, &C., occupied by Mr. R.Fairclough,. Mr. T. W. Clark, and Mrs. 41'. Rowson. A little• to, the Thelwall side of Cross-lane, and near to the resi- dence of Alderman l!ickniere, the new railway will reach its highest altitude, as it will here cross-the Ship Canal by a viaduct 51 feet abtave the level of the ground, 72 feet above high water level at ordi- nary spring tides, and between 78 and 79 feet above the intended water level of the Ship Canal. The limits of deviation in this neighbourhood. include the house, Conservatories, and a number of out- buildings occupied by Alderman Pickmere, and, in fact, almost extend to Thelwall-road. From the viaduct the new railway will descend by -the same gradient that it has risen-1 in 135—until it rejoins. the old 11,ne, as before stated, almost opposite. Thel, wall vicarage. .
