RUNCORN. RURAL . SANITARY AUTHORITY. .The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present. Colonel Ashton (chairman), the Rev. J. Lockwood,3lessrs.Aaron, Stokes, Brandreth, Hadfield, Wallington,. Mounfield, Hewitt, J. Whit- low, Lewis, W. Whitlow; H. Linaker (clerk), W. Linaker (deputy clerk),. field Farrington (in- spector). ' EXPENSES.. OF DEPUTATIONS. The following letter,was .read; signed Thomas Ellis : " Mr. Brunner, MX., desires me to, ask you to press upon the members of your.BOard the advisability of support- ing the action a the Association of' Local Boards with reference to the Local Authorities (Expenses of Confer- ences) Act, 1885. The framing of the regulations by the Local Government Board will not involve them in any expense, and will be a very great help to the Association, which has already done good work.' —The DeputrClerk said they had a similar communication addressed to the Autherity at Runcorn, and after discussing it they de- cided to let it lie on the table: It simply enabled the Local Government Board to sanction the expenditure of a deputation to meet and discuss local matters.—Mr. Aaron: Let it lie on the table.—Mr. Stokes: It does not concern us.—The Deputy Clerk: .Not more than anybody else.—Mr. Bra.ndreth said if the Authority wanted to send a deputation to London, it could pay their. expenses.—The Deputy Clerk said they could do that now for any legitimate purpose.—The matter then dropped.

FRODSHAIC warint SCIIBUB. The Deputy Clerk. read a report from a committee ap- pointed by the Rural Sanitary Authority to consider the provisions of the bill of the Frodsham Gas and Water Company. The committee had decided to ask the com- pany to make certain alterations in their bill, and if they did not consent to this request the committee recom- mended that the Authority should take such steps as would be necessary 'to secure the clauses they desired.— A letter was also read from the solicitors to the promo- ters of thitbill, stating. that they had carefully conai- dered the proposed alterations, and they could not ad- vise the-promoters to accept them. A draft letter had been submitted.to one or two of the Parliamentary Com- mittee, and they did not think there was any necessity for a meeting of the conaraittee.—The Chairman said that letter was practically a refusal of theeuggestions.— The Deputy- Clerk said there was really only one import- ant suggestion, and that was with regard to the water rates.—Mr. Hadfield said there was also the question of time; ten years wasa long time to have the matter hang- ing over. If the company did not do anything within that time they could still put their foot down and say nobody else should do it.—The Deputy Clerk said if the company did not proceed within ten years, or any time that might be required, and another company took the matter ups.this comiany would have to go to Parlia- ment,, and it would then be a question for the old com- pany: to say.whether they would do the work, or stand aside.and let the oth.er bill pass.—Mr. Hadfield said it was thought at the committee that ten year's was too long a time to leave it in suspense whether the thing should either be done or not be done. There had been no idea of putting any obstruction in the way of the com- pany,, for, as Frodsham went, it wa9 well known that water would be a very valuable thing, and would be a great boon to. the place. All they wanted to do was to take care that it was a fair and reasonable bill for the in- habitants,, and it was certainly thought that ten years was too long a time to enable the ,company to make. up their Winds. Then as. to wthe rate of remuneration, the company wanted power to charge as high as ten per cent on the rateable value, and even about 13 per cent if the water was brought 'from a certain reservoir. The-question really was, who was to oppose the bill ?—The Deputy Clerk said the Lord Presi-- dent of the Parliamentary Committee, the Duke of Buckingham, would be ,guided entirely- by precedent as to the powers that would be granted iunder the bill.— Mr. Hacipold said the only way to get the rates reduced was t(ooppose the bill, for if the Duke of Buckingham only had the company's side before him, he would natur- ally lean to their side.—Mr. Btandrath thought that Authority ought to take some action in the matter. Ten years was too low to have that matter hanging over Helsby and FrodsEam, and Relsby had plenty of water, —Tho Deputy Clerk: Have you not an epidemtc at Helsby.—Mr. Brandreth : I do net know about that.. —The Deputy Clerlasaid he understood there was some epidemic in Ilelsby.—Mr. Brandreth, said there had been no report before the Authority .--The Depti,ty Clerk said. there was a report for that day.. With regard bathe time allowed for supplying Fateh,, he explained that if that Authority passed a reaolutiien to supply water to Frodsham next year the.. company would have to stand aside unless they hadrcommenced.—Mr. Aaron agreed that ten years was too. long a period ta be al- lowed, and also that ten per cent was too high a.charge. —The Chairman said that what', they wanted to,do, was to get reasonable terms. They felt that the. works should be completed, as far as Frodsham was concerned, within three years. With regard to that objection he thought it was met totaarneextent by what Mr, Linaker had said to the effect that if the compiny did not move thit Authority could do so. But with regard to the rates to be charged for water, he thought they were much too high. There waa no doubt that if the bill passed entitling the company to charge 10. per cent, it struck him that it would almost be the ruin; of Prod- sham.—After some further discussion it was, agreed that the chairman should forward the objections of the committee to the President of the Parliamentary Com- mittee.

div.head: CLOSED, ROAD.
div.p: A CLOSED, ROAD.

In order to acquire as lively an apprehension as possible of the local alterations consequent on the construction of the canal, let the reader, in imagi- nation, project himself into the future of five or six years hence, or, at all, events, to a time suffi- ciently remote to have allowed of the completion of the canal and its contingent works. Having passed over the swing bridge that will by that time span the newly-made canal at Stockton Heath, let him suppose that he is making his way along the road past Wilderspool brewery to Warrington. In doing so he may note that the road which at present branches off opposite the Saracen's Head public- house for Daresbury. Preston Brook, and Chester, is then a cul-de-sac; that it is, so to speak, a mere "blind alley 'S leading past the northern walls of the brewery and a short distance farther, and then coming to a dead stop. At *hat exact point the road will be stopped it is not easy to predict. The Canal Company have acquired powers to close the road from beside the Stag Inn, Lower Walton, to a point thirty-six chains, or 792 yards, nearer Wil- derspool, measured along the road, and this includes the rdad for some distance on the Warrington side of Tom Paine's bridge. But whether or not the Company will close the road to the full extent that their limits allow may, of course, depend upon cir- cumstances which have not yet been foreseen. But as the Ship Canal cuts through the road a little on the other side of Paine's bridge, it may be anticipa- ted with some degree of confidence that the pre- sent road will cease f,cr be a thoroughfare at some point on the nearer side of that bridge.

ANOTHER NEW ROAD. But, pursuing our journey towards Warrington, on getting along Wilderspool Causeway to just within the borough boundary.it may be noted that an en.- tirely new road strikes off to the right in the direc- tion of Knutsford-road, through what are at present somewhat low-lying but green and almost park- like meadows. This new road is not part of the Ship Canal Company's undertaking, but will be the work of the Corporation of Warrington. In the Ship Canal Act it is laid down that the Company shall, before commencing the deviation ot the War- rington and Altrincham Railway—of which more .hereafter—give written notice of their intention to tile Corporation, and if within three months of such an intimation the Corporation give.notice that a new road is about to be made between the Latch- ford road and the Wilderspool Causeway—that is to say,•the road we are speaking of —the Company 81411, at their own cost, build a bridge through the new railway embankment to accommodate such road. It may here be remarkefithat at its last meeting the Warrington Town Council 'resolved that the notice on their part referred to should be `given to the Canal Company, so that it may be taken as pretty certain that the laying out of this new road will be proceeded with either contemo- poranepusly with the deviating of the Altrincham railway, or soon afterwards. The point at which the proposed road will pass under the railway will lig agreed upon. at the time of the laying of the new embankment,between the engineer of the Canal Company and the borough surveyor, but, as to the kind of roadway that has to be provided, it is ex- pressly laid down in the Act that 'the said bridge shall be constructed of a width between the walls thereof of not less than forty feet measured on the square, with a clear headway throughout the whole width of the roadway of not less than sixteep leet ; and the parapets of the said bridge shall be'carried 1 up to a height of not less than six feet." As to the prudence and foresight of the Corporation in making timely provision for this new road, there can scarcely. be two opinions. At present, as we know, all traffic, vehicular and otherwise, through Stock- ton Heath and Wilderspool to Warrington has to pass over the level crossing on the Causeway. As thin igs go now, this s inconve- nient enough at times, as the closing of the gates to keep a clear course for passing trains often leads to awkward blocks on market and other busy days; but, with the vastly greater traffic which the making of the docks on the Wilderspool side of the crossing is sure to cause in the future, the evils of blockages and congestion of traffic would be more and more seriously felt were there no other outlet' provided. The new road is therefore projected mainly for 'the purpose of meeting, as far as pos- sible, this difficulty, though it is evident it will be of advantage in other respects, and more particu- larly so should—and it is noimprobable contingency —streets of houses begin to spring upon the Wilder- spool side of the railway embankme t. It Is probable that the new thoroughfare will open out into Knutsford-road somewhere in the neighbourhood of St. Mary's-street, so that vehicles and passengiers from the, inward parts of Cheshire which make use of it in order to reach ,the centre of Warrington willhave to pass down St. James's-st. to the bridge over the Mersey, which is the sole connect- ing roadway between ,the Lancashire and Cheshire parts of the borough. It may, perhaps, be argued by some that if the traffic of the future increases to the extent that is anticipated the laying down of a new real will only half meet the necessities of the case. It will, if we may use the figure, enable the drivers of vehicles to escape the Scylla of the level crossing only to leave them as helpless victims to the Charybdis of a narrow bridge which is barely commodious enough for the traffic of to-day. And it does not need any great amount of prescience to foiesee that if the intended mew docks become the centre of evert a tithe of the business they may be fairly expected to do, one of the most pressing needs of the future will be the providing of a new, or an enlargement of the old, connecting link be- tween the two sections of the town. But though the building of a new bridge may be one of the re- moter consequences of the Ship Canal, the subject is one which scarcely comes within the scope of these articles, which deal more with what, humanly speaking, is to be than with what may be. A DEVIATED RAILWAY.

An object ;which, in the future, will loom large in the eye of a person passing along Wilderspool Causeway to Warrington will be the railway em- bankment, which will gradually rise higher and higher from the ground as it runs in the direction of Latchford station. This will be the new line of the present jow level railway from Bank Quay and Arpley stations to Lymra and Altrinchara ; in other words, the deviation railway No. 3 of the Ship Canal Act. This deviation of the existing liue is rendered necessary by the fact "that the line has to be carried over the Ship Canal by a high level viaduct—similar to that to be wade between Bank Quay and Moore—at a point near Cross-lane which runs from Knatsford-road to Thelwall-road

Davies, Stanton, Jeans, Reynolds, Geddes,Baishawßlease, Edgar,Adams, Chorkiy, W. Woods, Green, E. Dun,, John White, Miss Clara Harvey, Miss Pierpoint, Miss. Jones, Rev. G. B. Wray, Mr. John Roberts, and Mr. T. Cawley.. Subscrip- tions were alao given by Mr. Cox, Mr. Fletcher,. Mr. Paterson Mr. IL B. White, Mr. Low, and Mrs. Cromp- ton. The proceedsare to be devoted towards a. fund for providing prizes for the Sunday sq,hool children.—After tea the chair was taken by Mx. PBTER STUBS,, who, in opening the proceedings, said that that te&party marked the second year of their present vicar's mnlistry among them, and he had no doubt that by this time they had found out something of Mr. Wray's worth. (Applause.) I There was a little matter. which he was told. was no 'secret amongst them, and would come to the, front be- fore very long, and that was that they were likely to have an assistant vicar—if not a superior one. (Laugh- ter and applause.) That, too, he had no doubt all of them knew how to appreciate, and would do so most fully. (Applause.) The work of that district parish, he added, had been going. on, for the time he had mentioned, and, he thought, with considerable effect. (Applause.)A --The Rev. G. D. WRAY remarked that itwas cuatomarg on these occasions for the clergyman of the parish to give some account of the work which had been clone during the past year, and he wasglad to be able.to report some progress both in their parochial work and also in the endeavour to obtain that which the parishioners of St. Peter's had so long and earnestly desired, namely, a, church. (Applause.) And although he could not tell them anything more about the church than they already ..knew, he might say that as soon as ever a suitable site had been obtained the committee would meet once more for the purpose of raising the *money that was needed to complete and earry out that great, necessary, and im- portant work. (Applause.) Atipresent they had money paid into the bank, and promises amounting to over £2,000 ; that was, of course, including the £1,500 pro- mised by Sir Gilbert Greenall. (Applause.) He knew there were some of the parishioners who despaired of everhaving a church, but to such he would say, "Donot despair, Have Patience yet a little longer, and the church will come." (Applause.) The Sunday school had very much improved during the past twelvemonths, and the average attendance was now doable what it was at this time last year. (Applause.). For that he had to thank the Stinday school teachers, who by their regular and punctual attendance had taught thescholars the same important lessoo. (Hear, hear.) The report of her Majesty's Inspector on the examination held in their day school in October last was erninentllr satisfac- tory, and they obtained the same grant as in the pre- vious year, viz..„ 15s per head. (Applause.) He was, however, sorry to say that their school was not self-sup- porting; but it was hardly possible for an infant school te be self-supporting, because the fees, like the infants, were necessarily small. They had also had other diffi- culties, such as the fever epidemic and the opening of Hamilton-street Schools, to contend with. From these causes a loss a about 2,30 was sustained in the Govern- ment grant, and he renhtted that they had been unable , to cover that deficit ° by subscriptions, as everyone seemed to be so hard up nowadays ; still, he trusted that someone would come forward and relieve them of their difficulty. (Applause.) A mothers' meeting had been opened at the Girls' Club in John-street, and the work had been kindly undertaken by Mrs. Willcocks and Miss White, and to show how much the institution had been appreciated, he might mention that although only six or seven meetings had been held, there were al- ready 61 namee on the books, and there had been an average attendance of 40. (Hear, hear.) The thanks of the promoters were due to those ladies and gentlemen who had so kindly subscribed to enable the work to be , commenced and carried on. (Applause.) In conclusion he expressed his obligation to the friends who had SG generously subscribed, to the various works carried on in the parish, and to all who had assisted, or were about to' assist in that evening's proceedings. (Applause.)—The Rev. S. WILKINSON in a brief address expressed his plea- sure-at the satisfactory nature of the statement which had been made by Mr. Wray, and a hope that the desire of the parishioners in the direaiou of a chunk would

"Shakespeare and other Lectures," by Mr. George Dawson. M.A., is the title of a goodly volume of over 500 pages, edited by Mr. George St. Clair, F.G.S., and published by Messrs. iiegan Paul, Trench, and Co. These who have ever had the delight of listening to a lecture by the late George Dawson will not need to be told that a volume of this kind,is a treasure in its way: The only regret that can be experienced 'in perusing the work is that some of his inTmitable ',essays—for such they really are—were not report id: in full at the time they were given as -lectures. About one-fourth of the fifty or sixty. lectures are devoted to iShake- speare ; the rest are on very various sus, .such as literary forgeries and impostures.; old 15bolm; old tires and old ways; Samuel Pepys and hisdiary;• I French memoirs; ill-used men; the relations of great men to women; the study VGerman literature; music ;24 the relations 'of poets, painters; and, musicians; free libraries; national education; Voltaire, Roseau ; Benvenuto,. Cellini,, Ste:. Btc. What to many would seem the unpromising:title of " Thing. Unseen" is the subject of a series of four lectures, which may be -especially •commended to young thinkers who are grasping their way in a metaphysical fog, George Dawson was always reverent in dealing with the mysteries of life; but at the same time he was always bold, manly, and free from cant. .Hilw suogetteive are such sentences as ;—"The true miracle is always the overcoming of Matter by Spirit, and the • determining of matter, not by its outward laws, but by the spiritual laws which originally gave it birth ;" again—" What a difference is there in the sound of a law the day before we have broken it•and the day after l‘ We would not have j.t supposed that the lectures are what is termed heavy;reading ; on the cottrary, they are light in touch whilst handling, sometimes, the gravest of subjects. No one has a keener eye than George Dawson:for the humorous side of a situation. How neatly, he hits off:Rous- seau's love of notoriety when he says •He went away for retirement, and was angry when he even retired; he pretended •to forget the'world l sand. was savage when he.found the world had fOrgotten him." The lectures abound in ( such fine strokes. They are, therefore, stimulating, and at the same time healthful and instructive. "The Lyric of a Hopeless Love" is a poem of great length and of considerable merit by Mr, A: Stephen Wil- son. It should perhaps be described as a series of poems on one subject, but all in the same stanza: It is a sort of "In Memoriam" of "Rejected Addresses," and it is written with a sustained energy. which shods that Mr. Wilson has had hisleart in the work. The introductory sonnet described as the "key' note " is stiff and artifi- cial; it is so much inferime to the •rest of the work that the author does -himself an injustice •by giving it such prominence. There are readers who will conclude, that being the key note, that there is nothing to tempt them • to go further. Welave however read on, and have been pleased with the felicity of • illUstration, - and grace of diction which :are occasionally to be found. We give the following stanza as a fair specimen .of the work :

It needs no ceremonialdies , To bind my life to thine;: The bond already holds the prise By ordinance divine The blossom asks no other light ' Than, that which makes its petals bright In every spot and line, And what should I implore, above The charm which US my soul with love? It should be added that the " Lyric oh Hopeless Love " is handsomely issued by Mr. Walter &oat London. It looks quite poetical in its binding - of pale green and blue and gold.

A wollmoWn, elderly-. nobleman, of barge vi'eallth; wooed and won,, a few years ago, a young and verY beaudild: girl. Their life has been as happy as it is pos- sible 4or married life to, he, when December is united to Mar.. PIS lordship is-. distinguished hi scientific circles anot Pos.kosses high literary attainments.. Some time after his marriage he was fed's!), enough to think that his lovely wifewas not sufficiently educated, and laid out a coarse of reeding for her. A month, later he inquired about her progress, and found that she had not opened a boola. Beset up his eye- brows after the manner of old husbandh when their • young L rivoa have displeased them. WhereAtpois she locked up at him with a bewitching smile, and said "I , I was made to be loved, not to be learned.' She won tap day, of course. What Ifs learning'compared, to the light of a sunny blue eye? Would 'nob a husband rather be met with a smite and a kiss, than by a wile who assured him that she "knew her lesson ?" Wisdom La all very wall,, but winning vfays go further. Laughing , oyes beat Greek roots all to nothing. A woman's lovely tresses, waving, on the outside of tier shapely bead, are more precious in a husband's eyes than ever so much learning in side of it. went to the Pu blic all last Wednesday with theAntantion-of-speeking some • lEr -or-20 reinntee ~about the present Tory policy of Coercion. In following the ingenious argument of this or that leader in the political battle-field, we present ; grgtt to-ourtnerif . oiti that,at I,imes.itr refuges to. aceept all we effer. In theie eases the result is .a blur. oflalfrformed ideas, - "instead of a series ot distinAt 'impressions, and im- portant points may be oyerligoked which,should be borne in mind When forrning an Opinion that will gnide.us in giving our flex ;t vote upon the Irish question. It therefore' seems to Me that it is well ifocleaSionally we retire awhile from the noise Of disputation, and endeavour to take, 'in 'the qtfietneSs 'of thought, and Section i by. sec- "tip, asgeneral a view as we can of the more mpor- . Sane Of the large array of facts and arguments * vrhiehe tuider each branch of the Home Rule ques- tion; is suhraittedto our judgment.' IS elf, then, Without further preliminaries, what is at present thefriin and method of our opponents? Their present object is, no doubt, first of all to enforce obedi- ence to the law as it now exists in Ireland; and to pre- iienflthe commission of crimes created by the Coercion Bill of 1887. But, behind this, they have another oi- jebt. As long as the Irish agitate for Home Rule, -and as long as It is refused .to them, there cahnot be peace lon the other side of St. George's Channel. But without peace, prosperity is impossible. Therefore, assuming that ultimate peace is desired by our opponents as much as by ourselves, since they will not grant any measure of Home Rule to the Irish, they must have made up their minds to crush the deman4 for it. This is no doubt pretty generally accepted and understood to be their object, but there is considerable diversity of opinion as to how it should be attained. A year or a year and a half ago, it was to be got by conciliation; by simultaneity, similarity, by uniformity of Government throughout Great Britain and Ireland. 'Now all this is dropped by the leaders both of the Liberal Unionists and of the Conservatives. A measure of

Local Government for Ireland was admitted by them to be necessary, yet Ireland is to be excluded from the ' Local Government Bill which is to be introduced into .Parliamenl. Why ? Because decentralisation is ealeulated to'foster a spirit of Nationalism in Ireland, which, as being bound up with Home Rule, must not be encouraged. Ws say that it is impossible for the Government of Ireland to be carried on in a satisfaetory manner, nnlAs.• •the national aspirations of the people are recognized. Dirt' Hartington on the other hand has .made up his mind that he will not consent to the establishment of any. GoVernment which is founded upon these national aspirations. Therefore he no doubt considers himself bound to do nothing by which they will be encouraged, and therefore bound to refuse them Local Government. • But there is another reason for denying it to thd Irish. They are not fit for it, because as Mr. Goschen says— speaking perhaps fisruratively—they have become luna- tics. To this objection the obvious reply is that they were as much lunatics when the Local Government was promised them as they are now, and the promise either Was made in bad f4aith, or ought to be fulfilled. Further, if., they are lunatics to-day, will they ndt 4 the same 20 years hence? If so, can our Liberal Unionist friends give us any idea as to when it will be possible to adopt a policy of Concilia- tion instead of Coercion? The Tories tell us that.lrishmen,when they see that the Majority in this country have determined to resist their demand and to resist it by force—will cease to ask for Uoine demand', Those that talk that way rather under- estimatethe spirit of the Irish people. If anything could have broken that spirit. hi which is combined the tenacity of the Teuton and the fire of the Celt, the oppression of the eighteenth century would have done so. But after all that terrible tyranny, and after 87 Coercion bills in this Century, it is as strong as ever. Is it then altogether reasonable to suppose that they will now give in at the bidding of Lord Salisbury and Mr.Balfour,eveathoigth they are backed up by nearly all the Tory party, a nil for the moment still supported by a number of Liberal Unionist M.P's ? One strong argument there is, urged by tke more reasonable of illbse.who hold that the granting of Home Rule is both objectionable and unnecessaru. It, is that under good government in the future, the Irish will cease to ask for it. Lord Hartington says, whatever has been the casein the past with an- extended franchise, and with more perfect representation, Parliament is zone at any rate prepared to govern the people better. But would that government be in accordance with the views of the Irish..members ? While better in the opinion of the Toriestin the opinion of these others it might be worse. nor WA Parnell's Land Bill treated in 1888 ? The opinion of the Irish members, skilled as it is in respect to their own affairs, was then ignored. The Bill was thrown out, and no end of evictions, of suffering, of in- justice was the result. But supposing the House of Commons, legislating , wisely, did pass good measures when they were wanted, •whot guarantee have the Irish that the Lords would not impede and maul them Ais their custom? I believe that stir ont Of the last eight Loi•d:Lieutenahts have beeni or become Home Rulers; and surely if Lord Spencer te4usthat Irish affairs are miermanraged, or shelved, at Westminster, when both efficiency and promptitudeare required, we may. attach immense importance to his opinion: Lord Hartington may claim for future Gov- 4errfirfent3 good intentions, and .greater sympathy with the Irish than in the past, but it is not merely a question Of good intentions. After the famine which visited Ire- sand *1.848 or 1849, was there none felt towards this people of that unfortunate country? •Yet we have not in thelast'4o years succeeded in our government there. We have governed not according to Irish, but according to English ideas of what is best. We hate not had the .51/fArt or sympathy of the people, consequently we have failed. And still the old—as Johnliright has called it—" the ever failing, ever peisonons remedy of coer- cion" has been ipplied. As it has been before, So it will -be iti the future, if the Tories have their way, • Already the conciliatory policy of 1888 has been repii- ;Rated, and they are now going in for steady coercion". "Eluclideings cannot commend themselvts to Liberal Unionists.; and there are few indeed of this party who Will admit to their friends, or one would think td' them- selves, that Coercion is to be continuous and indefinite. Some there are who face the situation. Mr. Frodd, the historian, writes that the Isish are our natural enemieS

- -- . and cannot be governed by ordinary constitutional methods. I believe these are his sell, words, and at any rate they give the substance' of- his view. A hundred year, ago, perhaps still more reeen,tly, the -Irish might almost have been called the taturalenemies of this coun- try' and if to-day all Englishmen persisted in treating them its "rebels " and "Ilintentots;" it is most certain thac they would•hate Englishmen asi Englishmen: But •i isapue tiling to hate English government, and another stub be.irrecomilable foes of the people. The great de- I Amisstration in Dublin the other week showed how reedy thlpi/eofie gilieland will be to shake hands when Ire are prehared to treat them as friends. The advocates of a thorough policy ridicule these notions as sentimental nonsense,- and at least they are doing their best to make • the Irish rebels. Enfontinately it is lzecoming every day more plain that there' are...great numbers who are so,pre- J judiced against the and who entertain such a • hatred to Hornellule that, lather than grant it, they are ' prepared to p,t) any length -in tie way of Coercion. 'As Lord Hartington would say, they have countetlthe cost and have made up their minds to support Salisbury's programme of twenty years—he might as well ...have said anothar 2:89 years—of Coercion.

_ 'Bu t A is arso becoming clear that the present coercion is not severe enough for them. There is abundant em dence that the streuffit of Irish Nationalism is increas- ing rather than diminishing. If our opponents are W have a chance of achieving their object, they must be more' thorough. The Liberal Unionists see this, and nri: doubtedly it will lead to more of them adopting the general policy of the Liberal party. They know now' what they have known for some time past, but what we did not all realize in 1886, viz., 'that there is no alterg.. native taself-government except zoercion. Most-of-them will not endure the miserable prospect of continually governing Ireland by soldiers and constabulary. Of c6ercisn- ems,' 8i,16 laid enough and more th-iri" enough ; lbut unfortunately the.' bulk' of 1 the Conservative party are not yet satisfied,. !and are still true to their old policy of force.— Oc- casionalky one midi TYRE-ad outspoken gentleman of this party who in his enthusiastic ardour for the support of law and order, in his hat,red If. the Irish for resisting them, would send a regiment of. soldiers--or rather let one of tpose wfiicii we have to keep in the country— blow some of them to pieces. •peophsregard every detail of tur Constitution, everrlaw; . whether it be just or unjust, whether it has the support of the People, or whether it is dangerous and insidious and defied by the people; -does seem, to say the least, 'illogical. The prenounced Tory,. however, thinks differently. There are in Ireland moral wrongs for which there is no legal remedy. .But though he will denounce tyranny abroad, hewill not admit the necessity for any change in the law at home. What, then, are the tenants to do? They resort to-combination. That has been made illegal, and Mr. Balfour has thrown the whole weight of the Government on the side of the landlords, enabling those who are hard to do their worst. This is the way in Which they expect to teach the tenants to respect tho law! What could be the result of this—of the prosecu- tion of priests of the religion of the country, of men like! O'Brien and Sullivan—except secret or open disaffection, societies and conspiracies as of old, if not indeed civil war, were it not for the hope which is given by the en- lightened policy of the Liberal party? As a natural result of their action, the Government are, of course, at loggerheads with the people, and so long as the thornragh policy is continued there is nothing for it but irnpnson- ment, if not powder and shot in addition. The result of such a policy, it is true, can only be ex- asperation and disaffection; but it seems as if the Tories did not care for the disaster which coercion ,lias brought in the past and will bring in the future. They will not hear of any other course, and of many it would I be little or no exaggeration to say that "To reason they , will not list, their ears they stop, their eyes they close, And blindly, deafly obstinate, force desperately their way from woe to woe." This at least they' would do if. they could. They are setting out in pursuit of a desperate object, one that Crom- well might have proposed to himself. But if they are to • have the faintest prospect of success, they must in that punt* employ Cromwellian means. Is it likely that they will he allowed to do so? Supposing that these means . were allowed to them, and that they beat all the records of the past, exterminating or expatriating, we will say, half the people, what would be the feelings in the hearts of the other half? Would that other half at length have become sane and reasonable and quiet ?t We may take it that they would not have any friendly feeling towards England; but would even then the split of the remnant be utterly broken? And if these suppositions be efaggerations is there no element of truth in them? %There has lately been published a book by Mr. Justin McCarthy entitled "Ireland since the Union." It does not strike one as being written in a very one-sided or party spirit, and some, perhaps all of the most impor- tant facts in it are corroborated by. ether writers; In- teresting it certainly is from beginning to end; the details are few but judiciously selected, and, short though the history is, it gives a graphic and complete if , a general idea of what the state of the country has been during this century. It should also enable some readers to estimate at their true value several of the fallacies that are continually trotted out and paraded as being insuperable objections to the granting of Home Rule. I shall say little or nothing of the les- sons this book may teach those who have been unaceittai•ited with Irish history. I must rather apologise forthe i nordinate length to which this letter has already been extended, and hurry on to the end: There are, however, two chapters in • Irelartd since the Union," to which I should like to draw the , attention of your readers. One is headed John Brigla and John Dillon ;" the other the "Penal Laws!'.- The first gives us Mr. Bright's opinions 20 and 40 years ago on thE Government of Ireland by England during this century. The other tells us of penal laws which were enforced during the eighteenth eat tury. Of these most of us have only learnt what we have gatherea from the fragmenary references which in English histories are made to Irish affairs. Burke &d- -eems these laws as "unparalleled pppression," and Mr. McCarthy quotes Mr. Leeks' as saying of them that they were in the end " crushedby their own atrocity." There will be few readers *ho will not agree witls these opinions, and -as few who will think that sucif laws ought to have been supported or carried out by the Irish. Had I the history by me 'should have been tempted to .quote a few paragraphs avrice having it, I will merely poll out that at the end of the eighteenth century the spirit of the Irish was not broken, and that in spite of bribery and the grpatest misery and oppression the mass of the people still held fast to the tenets oetheie I faith, and that the desperate efforts to destroy the spirit of nationality, to make the people English, had avowedly failed. • Once more then ; what would be necessary if the pre- sent policy were in the end to attain to even partial suc- cess—really succeed in the true sense of the word, it never could? That is a serious question, and one which many Liberal Unionists, frons the highest to the lowest, shirk and evade. So far I have tried to show that coercion is inexpe- dient. Now, to take a higher standpoint. We. have abundant evidence of the spread of Nationalism in Ire- Land: Is it desirable, that, as coupled with the Mome Rule demand, we should attempt to crush that spirit? net,inlir.GladstoniSswords,its loss one of theheaviest, the most deplorable and the most degrading which a nation can suffer? Have we, as a nation, the right to at- tmp,t.to inflict upon Ireland that loss, to say nothing of the miseries involved in such an attempt? %%conclude ; aS far as our connection with Ireland goes, it is essential to the welfare of England, as it is both right and expedient, that there should be established m the sister kingdom a popular government. But if, for this reason, self-government is granted, it will be given upon other grounds as well. To be selfish is to be human. We are all afflicted more or less with the same disease, ' bet if we are Selfish it does not follow that we must be there- fore heartless. If the Trish peasantry are physically and in- tellectuallyJaelow what they ought to be, we have learnt in the last few years why this is so, and we may feel honest lymPathy for that hopeless, voiceless, lifelong nfleery, that has been the portion of such vast numbers in Ireland—for the suffering that saps alike both brain and body. 'There is no panacea which will imme- diately or shortly obliterate and annul all the evil which he so lthge`a degree is due to past misgovernment and oppression. • The effects of social disservices live after thm ;but se also does the energy of each social service, like the unending stream of one of nature's forces. It is our duty to perform one of these services towards Ire- land, -toisstablish the golden era of peace, and to lay the foundation of welt-being in the future. To us it is given. Ito-note the mighty ruin of the past. By the very ' thought of 4 we shall be irresistably impelled to make ' amends in the future :and someyamends we can make. We can behave towards Ireland in a way which, tir I may use the language of the greatest of our masterewill enable us in some degree at least to minister to a mind diseased, pluck the sorrows that are rooted hr the memory, an to raze out the troubles' that are written • in the brain- . • A. 11. SNOWSTORM IN SWITZERLAND.—A terri,ble snowstorm, such as has not been seen for several years, is taking 'place in Switzerland. In seveml cantons the snow is sederal -mitres high, and avaltuiches,', unfortunately ,accompanied by loss of life, are frequent; In the Can- ton of Uri an express train was blocked on Wednesday morning for over an hour in the St. Gothard tunnel, an avalanche having completely blocked its outlet.

The Engineer reported to the Gas and Water Commit 4 tee that during the last oix months no less than 72 lamps had been wilfully broken, and it was recommended that two boys be prosecuted. The mean rainfall fort the month had been 1.510 inches, and the water in stock on the 25* January was 8,761,778 gallons. The illumina- ting power of the as during the month had averaged 17-42 candles, and it was recommended tfiat an indepen- dent person be employed to test the gas. Correspon- dence bet Ween the Engineer and the Huyton-with-Roby Local Board respecting the laying and the level of the pipes for 'conveying the drainage from the Sewage Farm to the Netherby brook was submitted. The Committee not being satisfied with the way in which thb work had been done, recommended that a copy of the correspon- dence be sent tc. the Local Government 'Board. •—• Mr. Gaskell, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said they had heard a great deal about bad gas lately, and although the Committee thought the. complaints were without cause, they had recommended that an independent per- son test the illuminating power of the gas. Widnes, where the gas was only 17 candles, had been compared with Liverpool, where the gas was 22 candles. -Live. pool was the best lighted town in England, and it was not just to compare Widnes with that town. They Could supply 20 eandle gas in Widnes biat not stare price they did gas of 17 candlepower. ?It was for the public to say whether4hey were satisfied with that quality of gas.—Mr. Wright seconded the motion which was carried; MATERS.

Seventeen deaths occurred amongst children under one year. Zyinotic diseases caused two deaths, and there were two inquests.—The Nuisance inspector reported that the case of small-pox at 28, Terrace-road terminated fatally. No futher case had been reported. The Bench confirmed the appointment. Tua SALVATION ARMY.—On Saturday afternoon, th members of the local Salvation Army, aided by a con- tingent from WaiLlagton, conducted a service I throughout the streets of the village. A tea was after- wards provided at the barracks, but there was a poor I attendance.

• MUTUAL IMHROVEMENT ASSOCIATION. —On Monday evening the weekly meeting of the Lynun Mutual, Ink.. provement Association was held in the Wesleyan School toom. ,Mr. Brown presided, and there was a fair atten- dance. 'fr. Upson read a paper on "Th%Puritan.s," and a long discussion en.sued. WARBURTON PARISH CHURCEL—A very handsome stained glass east window, representing scenes in the Passion and Resurrection of our Lord, has just been fixed in Warburton new Parish Church. The window is the gift of Mrs. John Worthington, of Whalley Range, Manchester, in memory of her husband, who is buried at • Warburton. _ _ _

AT THELWALL.—OR Monday, a man named Fre'd Orainger was admitted into the Warririgton'ilnfir- ntaty,-suffeleing *oats broben leg:- It appears that he got off the 8-25 train from Warrington at Thelwall on Sunday-night slightly the worse for drink, and, after- wards fell into Hie Thelwall Brook, breaking his leg. He managed to crawl outrof the brook, and got into the PM- fold at Thelwall, where he remained until six, o'clock on Monday morning, when he was discovered, and subse- uently was conveyed to Warringtoi Infirmary. -THE CHURCH TOWER.—On Saturday afternoon a meet- ing was held in the vestry of the Parish Church to con- sider the matter of repairing the tower of the church. The Rector presided. The architect, Mr. J. S. Crowther, who was unable. to be present through indisposition, sub- mitted a report, in which lie advised the erection of a new tower. After considerable discussion, a motion was ' agreed to appointing Mr. John Dewhurst, Mr. T. P. ' Norris, Mr. Colin Mclver, with the Rector, churchwar- ' dens, and sidesmen, with power to add to their number, a committee to consider the subject of the re-building of the tower, and the ways and means for doing so. Cameron (chairman), Dutton, Harrison, Brazendale, Forster, Gibbon, Rogers, Thoma- son, and T. J. Ridgway (chlrk). . THE SALE OF THE SEWAGE FARM.—Mr. Thomason pro- posed that the seal of the Board be affixed to the agree- ment between the Board and the Manchester Ship Canal Company in respect to the sale of the sewage farm.— Mr. Gibbon 'seconded, and it waaagreed to. THE CLERK'S RESIGNATION, ALC.—Mr. Rogers proposed, and Mr. Dutton seconded, Mtbat the resignation of the clerk, Mr. _Ridgway, be accepted, and this was agreed to.—Mr. Rogers next nuived, and it was seconded by Mr. Diitton,that Mr. Ridgway be appointed to the position of law clerk.—Mr. Brazendaje did not see what they wanted a' law clerk for'.'- The Altrincham'Board, which was a much larger One than :theirs, hail not a paid law clerk. If they.got a good sharp clerk and collector tloy would be able.to do without a law clerk. They did not require one at all, except in a base where there was any legal business, when he would call on Mr. Ridgway to transact it.—Mr. Dutton said, perhaps, they would be in a difficulty sometime by not being able to get ' anyone at ,a, time when he was required; unless they ' had a law clerkin tteadance.—Ehe Chairman said has experience told him they shoula always have a law ' clerk present at their meetings.—Mp. Rogers proposed, and Mr. Dutton Seconded, that Mr. Ridgway be ap- pointed law clerk,. at a galary, of £35 year.—Mr. Braz- endale moved an amendment to the effect that no law clerk be appointed, but in 'case any assistance was re- cpiired Mr. Ridgway should be appointed to transact business.—This met with no seconder. The proposition was put, swirl Messrs. Gibbon, Forster, Rogers, Dutton, and the Chairman (5) voted for it.. Messrs. Harrison, and Thomason did not vote. THE SALARY' OF THE' CLERK ANA COl,lxeron.--Mr. Thomason drew attention to,the, salary of the clerk and collector. He said they should be A little economical" and not spend the ratepayers' mirky in a manner in which it ought not to be spent, giving £3 for 21 or 3 days' work. Many first-class men would come for £lOO a year.—Mr. Cameron pointed out that they would have to advertise afresh.—Mr. Thomason thought the position had better be advertised afresk than give too big a salary for two days' work a week.—Mr. Ridgway said he would guarantee thht no olerk would do the work in three days, and would have no time left to fool away.—Mt. 'Thoma- son propoSed, and Mt. Brazendale seconded, that only £125 be given to Mr. RidgwaY's 'successor, instead of the sum advertised.—On being put' to the meeting, Messrs. Brazendale, Harrison and Thomason voted for the proposition, the remainder of the 'Board iotirigo against it. TICE APPLICATIONS FOR CLERISIIIR.'i—The Board then proceeded to Consider the applicationafor the position of clerk, accountant, and collector of rates, of which 30 had been received. Two gentlemen were selected, 'Mit " the ' final consideration was left over to an adjourneclospecial 'meeting of the Board. . The adjourned 'special meeting was held on Thursday evening, when there were present Messrs. Cameron (chairman), APpleton, Dutton, Rogers, Harrison, Brazen- dale, Thomason, Gibbon, Forster, and T. J. Ridgway (law clerks—The two applicants for the clerkship who had been selected to appear were present, viz. f—Mr. Joseph Toft. assistant clerk to the Knutsford Guardians, and Mt. W. Mullard, clerk to Messrs. Ridgway and Worsley, Warringtori. Botlvarididates having been be- fore the Board, Mr. 'Button moved, and Mr. Gibbon seconded, that Mr. Mullard be' appointed. Mr, 'Thome- son moved as an amendment that Mr. Toft receive the appointment, .and this proposal was seconded by' Mr. Harrison. On being put to the vote, Messrs. Thomason. Brazenda/e, and Harrison voted for the amendment, and the rest of the members for' the original proposal, which was agreed to, Mr. Mullard consequently receiving the , . appointment.'

The Bank rate of aiscount was reduced on Thursday from 3 to 2i per cent. HOPE OF EAntisiowN LODGZ OF GOOD, TAKPLAR9.— The weekly session of the members was held on .Mon- day evening, Brother John Taylor, W.C.T., presi- ding. There was a good attendance. The digest of business for the annual session of the Dis- trict Lodge at Liveillool was considered, and the Lodge representatives were instructed thereon. The election of officers for the ensuing quarter resulted as follows :--W.C.T.' Sister. M. Allison; W.V.T., Sister J. Whitty ; W Sec., Brother G. Clarke; W.F.S., Sister E. Clarke; W. Tress:, Brother B. Newman W. Chaplain, Sister E. Whitty ; W.M., Brother T. laartindale ;W.D.M., Sister. J. Clarke; P.W.C.T., Brother J. Taylor. The officers were installed by Brother John Watburton, L.D., assisted by Sister M. E. Clarke, W.M.

TURNING A DRUNKEN WIFE OUT OF TER Houss.—Be- fore Colonel George McCorquodale, Mr. R. Houghton, Captain Withington, Messrs. T. J. Gillespie, A. C. Mc- , Corquodale and C. Pilkington, Thomas Hughes and Elizabeth Hughes, man and wife, were surrimoned for committing a breach of the peace by being disorderly on the 30th ult.—Elizabeth Hughes pleaded guilty, and Thomas Hughes not guilty.—P.C. Lloyd stated that he and P.C. Hughes saw_the female defendant near her own house fising filthy language and causing a crowd to as, semble. Witness asked her what was.the matter, and she complained that her husband had abused her and turned her out. Her son then came and took her into the house. Some time afterwards both her and her hus- band were falling out in the street and making use of bad language.—P.C. Hughes gave, similar evidence.— The male defendant stated that when he came home oft the night in question he found his wife had had some drink. 'As he did not like such things as that, be threw her outside. (Laughter.) Bia•wished to tell the. truth and nothing but the truth. Of course, his wife made a great noise, and the officer g came. Constable Lloyd came to the house an4asked if he (defendant) would take her in, and he said "ye." The constable asked "What must we do with ben" and he replied "no 'what you like with her." (Renewed laughter.) The constable then said if he did net let her xi he would re% port him. He was never off his own door step, and he never knew what he was being reported foruntil he got the summons.—The Chairman said that was a very sad case, and the Bench were sorry to sec a matt and wife in that position. He was sorry to say that the wife had been up very frequently, but it was not for some time past.—The ease against the husband would be disznissed but the wife would be bound over to keep the peace for three calendar months-in one surety of 15.
